en: Salutations to that Lord Jineśvara, the master of the bliss of knowledge, the divine among the learned, who is the sole benefactor of the world, for the sake of attaining one's own true self.

Now follows the examination of the truth of the teaching (*śāsana*). This very examination consists of the inquiry as to whether this [teaching] is logically consistent for him or not. And that consistency is possible only if the teaching is true, because it is precisely regarding its truth that there is dispute, just as in the case of the reliability of a speaker. It does not follow from the mere fact of being a teaching, because in that case [consistency] would be absent, just as in the case of the mere fact of being a speaker.

For here indeed there exist numerous systems of doctrine: the doctrines of the non-duality of the person (*puruṣādvaita*), the non-duality of words (*śabdādvaita*), the non-duality of consciousness (*vijñānādvaita*), and the non-duality of the variegated (*citrādvaita*); as well as the systems of the Cārvākas, Buddhists, followers of Śiva, atheists, Sāṅkhyas, Naiyāyikas, Vaiśeṣikas, Bhaṭṭas, and Prābhākaras; the doctrine of the sublation of all principles (*tattvopaplavaśāsana*); and the doctrine of manifoldness (*anekāntaśāsana*). Yet none of these can all be true, because they propound mutually contradictory meanings such as duality and non-duality, existence and non-existence, and so forth. Nor should one suspect that not even one among them might be true; for since absolute unity and manifoldness, duality and non-duality, or existence and non-existence, are mutually exclusive like light and darkness, a negation of both is impossible according to the rules of logic. Consequently, the affirmation of one must necessarily be established, and thus some truth must inevitably be admitted.

And thus, in that regard, one examines what indeed might constitute a true teaching. For this alone is the truthfulness of a true teaching: namely, its non-contradiction with what is perceived and what is accepted. If even that which contradicts valid means of cognition such as direct perception and inference were considered true, then nothing in the world would be false. Conversely, if even that which does not contradict them were considered false, then nothing at all would be true. Therefore, because it avoids the fallacies of under-extension, over-extension, impossibility, and non-existence, this definition of truth is observed to be faultless.

And since this quality of being non-contradictory with what is perceived and what is accepted exists only in the teaching of non-absolutism (*anekānta*), only that [teaching] is capable of ascending the throne of the true doctrine. Every absolutist teaching (*ekānta-śāsana*), however, is indeed entirely false, because it contradicts both what is perceived and what is accepted. To illustrate:
first, the teaching of the non-duality of the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahmādvaita*) is indeed contradictory to both perception and accepted tenets.

For this is the position of the proponents of Brahman: {1. Examination of the Teaching of the Non-duality of the Supreme Brahman} First, the non-duality of the Supreme Brahman is indeed in contradiction with both what is perceived and what is accepted. For this is the view of the Brahmavādins—

{1.1 Pūrvapakṣa} There exists only this one Supreme Brahman—unconditioned by space, time, or form, free from error, pervading all states, consisting of nothing but manifestation, and the undivided nectar of knowledge and bliss—and there is no second. This is because of such scriptural declarations as, "Brahman is one alone, without a second.

If it is asked, "How can there be only one Supreme Brahman, given that diverse selves, mutually distinct, are perceived? we reply: No, for even though it is one, it is possible for that [Brahman], abiding in every single being, to appear in manifold ways, like the moon in waters. As it has been said:

"But the single Self of all beings, residing in every being, is seen as one and also as many, like the moon in water" (Amṛtabindūpaniṣad 12). Thus, even earth and the other elements are not distinct principles from That, because they are its illusory transformations (*vivarta*). And this is because the birth and other states of this entire manifold (*prapañca*)—consisting of high and low, moving and stationary forms—proceed from That alone. This has been stated by the venerable Bādarāyaṇa: "From which [Brahman] the birth and so forth of this [world proceed]" (Brahmasūtra 1.1.2).

Now, if it is asked how birth and so forth can proceed from the Supreme Person, who effects the destruction of the determination of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), we say: no; for that [birth] exists from Him precisely because He is accompanied by beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*).

If it is argued that ignorance would then be a second entity, that is not so; for since it cannot be established within the domain of valid cognition through either the investigation of its existence or non-existence, it is *anirvacanīya* (indescribable). As it has been said:
"Of the Lord who is accompanied by the pair of indescribable ignorances..."

"We bow to that Brahman, which is immortal, consisting of immeasurable bliss and knowledge, from whom these— space, air, fire, water, and earth— are emanations, and from whom this entire universe, moving and unmoving, high and low, has arisen. (Bhāmatī 1)

If it is objected: "Even so, since duality exists within the transformations of the transformation (*vivarta-vivarte*), how can non-duality (*advaita*) be established? We reply: No; for these transformations, which are of the nature of *māyā*, appear within that [non-dual reality] just as the form of a snake appears in a rope. As it has been said:

"In that which, through delusion, the three worlds shine like a snake in a rope—though it is itself fearless—I am He, whose body is the eternal, untainted nectar, the supreme essence of transmigratory existence. (Source unknown)

This entire phenomenal manifestation appears only while ignorance (*avidyā*) exists, but not when ignorance has ceased. And that cessation of ignorance is itself liberation (*mokṣa*). The means for this is precisely the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman. That [realization] also comes about through hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditation (*nididhyāsana*). Thus says the Śruti: "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad 2.4.5). Likewise, the Smṛti says:
"It is to be heard from the words of the Śruti, and it is to be reflected upon by means of logical reasoning."
And having understood this, one should constantly meditate upon these causes for vision. (Source unknown) Thus it is said.

In this context, *śravaṇa* (hearing) is the determination of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the Upaniṣadic statements regarding the Supreme Brahman. *Manana* (reflection) is the investigation of the meaning thus heard through reasoning. *Dhyāna* (meditation) is the mental contemplation of the object ascertained through hearing and reflection. And that [meditation] is accomplished by one who possesses the fourfold means: discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities, the attainment of tranquility, self-control, and so forth, dispassion for this world and the next, and the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutva*). Upon that [meditation], there occurs the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman; and therein lies the attainment of liberation, characterized by union with the Supreme Brahman.
{1.2 Uttarapakṣa}

This teaching of the absolute non-duality (advaitaikānta) is contradicted by direct perception (pratyakṣa). For, through direct perception, there is the ascertainment of a manifestation of diverse external objects—distinguished by differences of place, time, and form, such as actions and their factors, or villages, groves, elephants, horses, and so forth—which are real in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), mutually excluded from one another, and which possess specific variegated appearances as their respective objects. Furthermore, because non-duality is contradicted by direct perception in which difference appears, for a perception of difference is logically impossible within that which is in every respect a single unity.

If it is argued that non-duality (*advaita*) is not contradicted by perception—since even in a single entity, the perception of distinctions between action and its factors (*kriyā-kāraka-bheda*) is possible, just as in the experience of a dream—this is not so. For even in the experience of a dream, since its unity remains, the contradiction [with perception] persists. Indeed, in that case, the perception of specific actions arising from one’s own latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is one thing, and the direct perception of specific causal factors is another; they are not one and the same, for that would entail the absurd consequence of there being no distinction in their respective causes, the latent impressions. Just as in the waking state, even in states such as dreaming, the person—who consists of manifold powers—is established through a variety of appearances of specific actions and causal factors. Furthermore, even for things like the self or space, which some maintain to be of a single nature, it cannot be proven that they serve as the objective basis for the appearance of multiple specific actions and causal factors according to the proponents of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*). Therefore, non-duality is indeed contradicted by perception.

If it is argued that this perception manifesting difference is erroneous, like the perception of a magical illusion (*indrajāla*) and the like, then this is even more erroneous, because the aforementioned defects have not been avoided. This is because, in any case, there is no possible example—whether of an erroneous or a non-erroneous perception of difference regarding a single entity—and thus such a perception is impossible. Furthermore, even if that [perception] were erroneous, the contradiction with non-duality (*advaita*) would remain as it was. Even what has been stated in some way is improper, because only the magical illusion and the like are erroneous due to the existence of a sublater (*bādhaka*). Indeed, even children and women understand that the perception of the distinction between action and its factors—such as "the potter makes a jar with a staff and so forth," or "the person eats rice with his hand"—is not erroneous, because there is no sublater for it. As it has been said by the venerable Bhaṭṭākalaṅkadeva:

They cause delusion regarding [illusory phenomena] such as Indra’s net, and nothing else—even for the eyes of the restless children of outcasts and cowherds. (Nyāyaviniścaya 1.51cd–52ab) If it is argued that even here there exists a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*), that is incorrect; for no means of valid cognition whatsoever is possible that could establish the non-duality of the supreme Brahman—which is otherwise than the distinct objects of perception. This is because only that which establishes a difference in the object can properly function as a subverter, just as the cognition of mother-of-pearl subverts the cognition of silver in the case of mother-of-pearl.

But is it not the case that perception alone is the means of establishing the Supreme Brahman? For immediately after the opening of the eyes, there arises a non-conceptual cognition whose object is the affirmation of pure existence (*sanmātra*), and since existence is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman.

Indeed, there exists an initial non-conceptual cognition of mere observation, similar to the cognition of infants, the mute, and others, which arises from the pure object itself. (Ślokavārttika, Pratyakṣasūtra 112)

If it is argued that this is because of such scriptural statements, that is all the more clearly contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For one never experiences that "mere being" (*sanmātra*) as described by others—devoid of all particularities, entirely eternal, partless, and all-pervading. Even immediately after opening one's eyes, one directly perceives only universals such as existence (*sattā*) as qualified by specific characteristics like being visible in a particular place and time. One does not perceive a seer who is not restricted to a particular place and is non-different [from the object], for otherwise it would entail the denial of what is actually experienced. Furthermore, it is impossible for the universal and the particular to exist in mutual exclusion, as in the case of a staff and the person wearing a staff or earrings; for if one of the two were absent, the other would also necessarily be absent. As it has been said:
A universal could not exist without particulars, just like a donkey’s horn;
and likewise, a particular would not exist if it were devoid of a universal.
Therefore, perception cannot establish the supreme Brahman; on the contrary, it would only contradict it, because perception apprehends both positive entities and their mutual exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).

Now, is it not the case that perception does not sublate non-duality, because, being affirmative in nature, it lacks the capacity for negation? The wise have said: "Perception is affirmative, not negative; therefore, the scripture concerning oneness is not sublated by that perception" (Brahmasiddhi 1.4).

If it is argued that this is because of such scriptural statements, that is incorrect. For it is logical that perception or scripture, which have as their object the prescription of specific things, can function as negators [of others]. This is because the cognition of a mere affirmation is itself of the nature of a cognition of the negation of anything else; for the cognition of a mere ground is established as being of the nature of the cognition of the absence of a jar. Indeed, this cognizer, while perceiving something, does not perceive it as mixed with other forms, such that the negation of those would have to be established by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, the restriction that only perception and Upaniṣadic statements are prescriptive is impossible; otherwise, it would follow that they prescribe ignorance (*avidyā*) just as they prescribe knowledge (*vidyā*). How can one who perceives pure Being (*sanmātra*) through the exclusion of ignorance—while asserting that "perception or anything else is not a negator"—be considered sound? Or how could he perceive the absence of negating power in perception and the like? For the very fact of that cognition establishes that its object is indeed non-existence (*abhāva*). If it is argued that the cognition of perception and the like as prescriptive is itself the cognition of the absence of negating power, then it is established that they have both existence and non-existence as their objects. And thus, since the absolute monism (*advaitaikānta*) is contradicted by perception itself, how could that [monism] ever be proven by it?

[Objection: Surely there exists an inference that establishes this [monism], namely: "Everything under dispute is included within appearance (*pratibhāsa*), because it is co-referential with appearance (*pratibhāsa-samānādhikaraṇatvāt*). Whatever is co-referential with appearance is included within appearance; for example, the very nature of appearance. And everything is co-referential with appearance. Since the reason (*hetu*) is faultless, the supreme Brahman, whose form is mere appearance, is established. [Response: This is like raising a weapon for one's own destruction by the proponents of Brahman (*brahmavādins*). For if, by the reason "because it is co-referential with appearance," everything is shown to be included within appearance, then once the non-duality of the Person (*puruṣādvaita*) is established, the duality between the reason and the probandum (*hetu-sādhya-dvaita*) becomes unavoidable. As it was said by the venerable teacher Samantabhadra: *(Note: The original Sanskrit text provided here is the argument of the opponent. The response and the citation from Samantabhadra would follow in the full source text.)*
"If the non-duality [of the reason] is established by means of a reason, then there would be duality between the reason and the probandum;
if, however, establishment occurs without a reason, why is duality not [established] by mere words? (Āptamīmāṃsā 26)

[Objection: Even if non-duality (*advaita*) is established by the reason (*hetu*), there will still be duality between the reason and the probandum (*sādhya*), because their identity (*tādātmya*) is admitted. Nor is there a contradiction in the relation of the probandum and the probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) when they are identical; for otherwise, one would have to admit a similar contradiction in the relation between existence (*sattva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*). If you argue that here, despite the difference between the properties of probandum and probans, there is no subversion of their relation because the distinction is merely a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), and thus even in the inference under discussion, how could there be an obstacle to the relation between the reason and the probandum—which are both imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*)—since in every respect there is no difference [between them], we say: No. For even in the case of existence and impermanence in sound and so forth, since their identity is only partial (*kathañcit*) and not absolute, their absolute identity is unestablished; if that were established, the relation of probandum and probans would be contradicted. Furthermore, this proof is not valid because it is contradictory (*viruddha*). Since there is some degree of difference between the appearance (*pratibhāsa*) and what is intended as its object, the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is perceived; therefore, the proof does not establish that the object is entirely absorbed within the appearance. Indeed, even in cases such as "the white cloth," co-referentiality does not exist if there were absolute identity between quality and substance, just as there is none between things that are absolutely distinct. Even in the statement "the nature of the appearance appears," there is no absolute identity between the appearance and its nature, which function as the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and the defined (*lakṣya*); for the appearance, as the locus of common and uncommon properties, is established as having some degree of difference from its own nature, which consists of its uncommon properties. Otherwise, it would be unfit for co-referentiality, like "gold is gold" or the relationship between the Sahya and Vindhya mountains. Thus, whatever is co-referential with the appearance is in some way an entity other than the appearance—just as the nature of the appearance itself; and since all things such as pleasure and blue are co-referential with the appearance, the reason proves the opposite of the probandum. Therefore, non-duality is not established.

If it is argued that there indeed exists scripture (*āgama*) that establishes this [non-duality], because there exists scripture such as "All this, verily, is Brahman" (*Maitrāyaṇyupaniṣad* 4.6), which establishes the Supreme Brahman—even that is merely raising a weapon for one's own destruction, since it would entail duality between non-duality and its scripture.
If, however, the view is held that scripture itself is of the very nature of the non-dual Person and is not distinct from Him—such that duality does not follow—it is said:
"They call the imperishable *aśvattha* tree rooted above and branching below. (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 3.9)
For it is said in the *Bhagavadgītā* (15.1): "He whose leaves are the Vedic hymns—he who knows him is a knower of the Vedas.

Consequently, like Brahman, that scripture would also be unestablished; for there is a contradiction in something whose nature is entirely unestablished being established, as this would entail a distinction between what is established and what is unestablished.

Furthermore, from such scriptural passages as "All this, indeed, is Brahman" (*Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad* 4.6), the establishment of duality itself would result, because that which is already established [as the world] is enjoined as having the nature of Brahman—which is not previously established—just as one cannot enjoin what is already established in every respect, as if it were unestablished. Since the nature of Brahman, which is of the form of identity, is established in some individual self and is then enjoined in all selves and even in those not admitted to be selves, how can there be the establishment of non-duality? Even if the superimposition of the manifold world of duality is excluded by that scripture, the existence of both the object to be excluded and the excluder is established; thus, how can non-duality be established? If the scripture has the nature of the Supreme Brahman, non-duality is not established from it, because the absolute identity of the nature and that which possesses the nature is logically untenable.

If it is argued that self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) alone establishes the non-duality of the person (*puruṣādvaita*), we say no; for this would entail a duality between self-awareness and the self. Indeed, even self-awareness as a means of proof cannot be non-different from the self, because that would contradict its status as a means of proof. Just like inference and scripture, it is only when something is distinct from the object to be proven (*sādhya*) that its status as a means of proof is possible; for, just as with the inference and scripture under discussion, there is an absence of the status of being a means of proof in the case of the perception of self-awareness as well.

Nor is the non-duality of the person (*puruṣādvaita*) established by itself, as is the case with the non-duality of consciousness (*vijñānādvaita*), because there is no self-evident cognition of its own nature; otherwise, it would be impossible for anyone to have a disagreement regarding it, and furthermore, it would entail the undesirable consequence of admitting the well-known non-duality of consciousness.

If it is argued that the non-duality of consciousness (*vijñānādvaita*) is not established by itself—because, being momentary, it lasts for only a single moment; and because, being partless, it consists of a single atom, such that there is no experience of it even once—then we say: no. For the same reason applies to the non-duality of the Person (*puruṣādvaita*): since it is eternal, pervading the entire collection of time, and omnipresent, being established in all places, there is likewise an absence of its experience even once. Furthermore, if you accept the position that "Brahman is established by itself," why would duality (*dvaita*) not also be established by itself, even in the absence of all means of proof? Or would [non-duality] be merely the sublation of reality (*tattvopaplava*), or the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmya*), since there is no difference between these and one's own mere assertion? Moreover, the fulfillment of every desire for everyone would become impossible to prevent. Thus, since there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever to establish the Supreme Brahman, the fact that perception—which grasps difference—is without a sublater remains firmly established, as no other sublater of this [perception] is possible.

It might be argued: "The perception and other means of knowledge under dispute are indeed false, because they manifest distinctions, like dream-perception and the like. This is incorrect; for in the inference under consideration, if the manifestation of the distinction between the subject (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) were not false, there would be a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the reason due to that very [manifestation]. If, on the other hand, that [manifestation] were false, the probandum (*sādhya*) could not be established by that inference. If it is argued that there is no fault because the manifestation of the distinction between the subject and so forth is not false according to the opponent's own admission; we say no, because there would be a fallacy of deviation due to the manifestation of the distinction between one's own and the opponent's admissions. If, because that too is not false according to another opponent's admission, there is no fault, then the same fallacy of deviation would occur due to the manifestation of that distinction; thus, nothing would ever be established.

Someone says: "Since there is no sublater (*bādhaka*)—such as perception of the distinction between action and its factors—for the non-illusory pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) which is the non-duality of Brahman and is self-established, those [perceptions] are erroneous; therefore, they do not contradict it. This too is not sound, because if that were the case, since there would be a distinction between the object to be sublated and the sublater, the consequence would be the establishment of duality (*dvaita*).

Nor does the relationship of the sublated and the sublater (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) between those two arise merely from the assertions of others, for that would result in the absence of such a relationship in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*). Therefore, since there is an absence of all sublaters, how could this difference, established by non-erroneous perception (*pratyakṣa*), not contradict non-duality (*advaita*)? [Objection: Precisely because of their mutual contradiction, non-duality should contradict difference. [Response: No; for non-duality is a mere assertion, as it has already been stated that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish it, whereas difference is established by valid cognition. This is because the perception that grasps it has been proven to be non-erroneous due to the absence of any sublater. Indeed, the mere assertion of someone does not negate the difference between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*) when it is established by valid cognition, just like the assertion of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*). Thus, since it is free from all sublaters, the difference between action and its factors, established by non-erroneous perception, is indeed contradicted by the position of absolute non-duality. Consequently, it is established that the teaching of the non-duality of the Supreme Brahman is contradicted by perception. As it was said by the venerable master Ācārya Samantabhadra:

"Even in the position of absolute non-duality (*advaitaikāntapakṣa*), the observed distinction between causal factors (*kāraka*) and action (*kriyā*) is contradicted; for nothing arises from itself. (Āptamīmāṃsā 24) By this very [argument], the teaching of non-duality is shown to be contrary to what is accepted, because it has been stated that duality is established by both inference and scripture which prove non-duality. Furthermore, there is a contradiction with inference, as in the following: "The word 'non-duality' (*advaita*) depends upon a real entity (*arthāpekṣa*) that is the opposite of its own denotation, because it is a negative compound (*nañ-pūrva-akhaṇḍapada*), like the expression 'non-cause' (*ahetu*). This too was stated by the venerable Svāmis:
"Non-duality does not exist without duality, just as a non-cause cannot exist without a cause; nor can there ever be a negation of a cognizer without that which is to be negated. (Āptamīmāṃsā 27).

Thus, for the proponents of Brahman (*brahmavādin*), the practice of religious duty (*dharmānuṣṭhāna*) finds no firm footing, because for them, merit and demerit, pleasure and pain, this world and the next, knowledge and its opposite, bondage and liberation, are all impossible—just like the proponent of the sublation of reality (*tattvopaplavavādin*). In the same way, the Master [Ratnakīrti] has said:
There would be no duality of karma, no duality of fruit, and no duality of worlds;
likewise, there would be no duality of knowledge and ignorance, nor the duality of bondage and liberation. (Āptamīmāṃsā 25)

By this, that which has been stated by the Vedāntins—namely, "Brahman alone is seen as manifoldness; the earth and other elements are transformations (*vivarta*) of Brahman; liberation is the attainment of Brahman; and the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman occurs through hearing [the scriptures] and so forth"—all of this deserves to be disregarded like a description of the beauty of a barren woman’s son, because there is no establishment of Brahman by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a duality between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge. If its establishment were by means of a deluded cognition, there would follow the consequence of establishing an ultimately real fire from smoke perceived in a dream and the like. Furthermore, since the perception of the moon occurs through a reflection that is ultimately real due to being a transformation of water-particles resulting from a specific proximity to the mass of moonbeams, if the non-duality of Brahman were established by a deluded cognition or without a means of knowledge at all, then the establishment of duality, selflessness, and so forth would likewise be unavoidable. Thus, because there is an absence of either a subverter (*bādhaka*) or a prover (*sādhaka*) for both duality and non-duality, the Vedāntins' abandonment of what is observed and the postulation of what is unobserved result merely in ridicule.

Furthermore, if there is only the one Supreme Brahman, why does that alone not enter the path of cognition? Or, if the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is non-existent in nature like the horn of a donkey, why then does that very [Brahman] appear in the path of cognition through the sense of "I, I"? When thus questioned, let the opponent clearly explain: if he says, "It is so because of ignorance (*avidyā*)," that is incorrect. For it is impossible to establish the nature of ignorance as described by the opponent, since it cannot escape the scope of conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*). If ignorance were non-existent, it could not logically be the cause of false cognition; for we observe that only existing things—such as unseen defects, mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), machines, mantras, and rituals—are the causes of false cognitions like dreams and magical illusions. If that ignorance were of the nature of existence, then duality would necessarily follow. If ignorance is "indefinable" (*anirvacanīya*) in terms of being either existent or non-existent, how can it be explained to a disciple that "ignorance exists during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) because the world is a manifestation of ignorance, but it does not exist in the state of liberation because liberation consists in the cessation of ignorance"? At that time, it would be possible to define it as either existent or non-existent. And if it is not so explained, how could those to be trained proceed toward liberation, given their lack of understanding regarding the true nature of transmigratory existence and liberation? To say "ignorance is indefinable" while describing the nature of ignorance is self-contradictory.
Just as it is said: "As long as I live, my father shall remain silent and a celibate student;

my mother shall never be barren, and you shall be like the god of love, incomparable. For if ignorance (*avidyā*) were designated by the term "ineffable" (*anirvācya*), it would result in a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) due to the utterance being meaningless.

Is it not the case that the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) applies only to real entities (*vastu*) and not to non-entities (*avastu*)? Therefore, we establish ignorance (*avidyā*) by taking into account the nature of real entities. As it has been said:
"If Brahman is held to be possessed of ignorance, then indeed this is a great fault. (175)
Furthermore, if ignorance were absent, the futility of knowledge would follow;
yet, while remaining within ignorance itself, one imagines that "this [person] has no ignorance. (176)
Ignorance cannot in any way be Brahman, because ignorance is experienced as "I am ignorant," just like the experience [of the self] as "I am Brahman. (177)
Therefore, that state of being otherwise (anyathātmatā) is also destroyed by the consciousness arising from the mind;
since it is sublated once Brahman is known, it is logically established that it is not ignorance (avidyā).
Moreover, when [reality] is thoroughly understood, false cognition no longer remains uncontradicted;
one who possesses ignorance is not capable of defining that very ignorance. (179)

Therefore, with regard to the actual state of things, it is not defined as "ignorance" (avidyā); for it is not logical for the operation of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to apply to anything other than a real entity (vastu). // 180 //
And ignorance is not accepted as a real entity because it cannot withstand the scrutiny of valid cognition;
moreover, this very [inability to withstand scrutiny] is the defining characteristic of ignorance's nature as ignorance. (181)
"Intolerance of honor and injury is held to be its unique characteristic.

(Saṃbandhavārttika 175b–182a) Furthermore, there is no fault whatsoever in postulating such an unproven ignorance (*avidyā*), because it resides within the experience of the transmigrating soul itself. For the proponent of dualism alone, there follows a manifold variety of faults in postulating the manifold of seen and unseen objects, which is sublated by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). As it has been said:
"In your position, much would have to be postulated, and everything would contradict perception. (182)

"According to my position, it is merely conceptual ignorance (*kalpyāvidyā*), and that is based on experience"—so says someone. He too is not a discerning person, because he accepts ignorance itself as having a nature that transcends all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For no discerning person accepts either ignorance or knowledge as having a form that lies beyond all means of valid cognition.

Nor is it incorrect for means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to have ignorance (*avidyā*) as their object, because ignorance, like knowledge (*vidyā*), is in some sense a real entity (*vastu*). If it is argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [ignorance] being knowledge, we reply: nothing undesirable follows, since it has been stated by the venerable Akalaṅka: "In whatever way there is non-discrepancy (*avisaṃvāda*), in that way there is validity" (*Siddhiviniścaya* 1.19). However, with respect to external objects of cognition, the fact that a certain consciousness is ignorant is determined by a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*). How could that [consciousness] not be an object of a means of valid cognition? Furthermore, that which subverts it is experienced precisely as a means of valid cognition that establishes the contrary nature of the object. Thus, ignorance must be defined solely with reference to the actual state of things (*vastuvṛtta*).

Nor is it in any way contradictory for the self, who is a cognizer, to possess ignorance even while possessing knowledge—since that would entail this great fault. Nor does the absence of ignorance in any way result in the futility of knowledge, because its fruit, which is characterized by all forms of knowledge, exists.

Nor can it be postulated that, while remaining in ignorance itself, one conceives, "This is my ignorance," because for everyone, the determination of the distinction between ignorance and its opposite occurs only in the state of knowledge (*vidyā*), whereas such a distinction is absent during states of ignorance such as dreaming. Therefore, it is illogical for ignorance to exist apart from the Self. For since the Self is the possessor of the experience "I am possessed of ignorance," it is precisely through that [Self]—which is not sublated by any cognition arising from a valid means of knowledge—that ignorance is also established as being that very same [Self]; thus, there is no contradiction with the nature of the Self. Nor is it untenable that ignorance exists even when the Self is known in some way, because there is no contradiction with sublation. On the contrary, it is all the more appropriate that ignorance exists even when the Self is known in some way, because it is only for one who has known the Self that the sublation of that [ignorance] is determined, and it is established that a cognition which is somehow sublated is false.

Furthermore, a person who is himself possessed of ignorance is in no way capable of defining that very ignorance, for that would result in the collapse of all the practical transactions of discerning people. As for the claim that the unique definition of ignorance is its inability to withstand the impact of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), even that must be ascertained precisely through the power of those same *pramāṇas*. Thus, there is no such thing as "ignorance" that transcends the *pramāṇas*; if one were to accept such a thing, it would contradict the non-duality of Brahman.
Thus concludes the Examination of the Doctrine of the Non-Duality of the Person.
{2. Examination of the Doctrine of the Non-Duality of the Word}

By this, monism of sound (*śabdādvaita*) is also refuted; for, like monism of the person (*puruṣādvaita*), it is established that it too falls within the scope of the faults already stated. This is because its systematic arrangement is untenable due to the mere difference in methodological procedure, because there is no distinction in the absence of either proving or subverting evidence regarding one's own position or another's, because self-establishment is impossible, and because there is no other alternative course—enough with this overly prolix discussion. For monism in every respect is established as unreal, being in contradiction with both what is perceived and what is accepted. [Thus ends] all the speech of the Vedāntins, resulting from the destruction of the proof of Brahman-ignorance (*brahmāvidyā*).
Because it would be mere idle chatter, it should not be heeded by the wise.
The doctrine of the non-duality of Brahman is not true, because it contradicts both what is perceived and what is accepted;
furthermore, it is certain that the doctrine of conditional predication (syādvāda) cannot be refuted by it.
Thus concludes the Examination of the Doctrine of the Non-Duality of Sound.
[3] Next, the doctrine of the non-duality of consciousness (*vijñānādvaita*) is contradicted by what is perceived and by what is accepted as valid.

{3.1 Pūrvapakṣa} For instance: this is indeed the position desired by the proponents of the non-duality of consciousness (*vijñānādvaitavādins*): that reality belongs only to internal cognition, which is self-cognized, and not to the external object, because an insentient thing cannot manifest [as such], and because the definition of the cognized and the cognizer as conceived by others is fallacious.

In that regard, first of all, the [three factors] postulated by the Sautrāntikas—namely, the arising of that [cognition], its conformity to the object, and the determination of it—are not individually the defining characteristics of the cognized and the cognizer; for they are subject to deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the eye, in the case of a cognition immediately following one directed toward the same object, and in the case of the determination of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. Furthermore, there is deviation in the case of a cognition immediately following a cognition of a yellow form in a white conch shell by one whose eyes are afflicted by jaundice or similar disorders.

Even the status of being a causal condition for an effect (*kāryanimittakāraṇatva*) as accepted by the followers of Yoga is not its defining characteristic, because it is over-extended (*anaikānta*) to the eye. Likewise, the capacity for origination (*prabhavayogyatā*) and so forth, known as the "causal relation" (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) postulated by others, is also not its defining characteristic, because it is contradicted by that very same [eye]. Consequently, since no definition whatsoever of the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the apprehender (*grāhaka*) is possible, all cognition consisting of the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender is indeed erroneous (*bhrānta*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever possesses the form of the apprehended and the apprehender is entirely erroneous, just like the cognition of dreams, magical illusions (*indrajāla*), and the like; and such is the case with perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other forms of cognition. For erroneous perception and the rest do not establish the existence of external objects, because it would follow that even the perception of dreams and similar states would establish the existence of objects. Thus, external objects, though seen, are not to be believed in when they are logically untenable. As it is said: "I do not believe in that which cannot be established by reason, even if I have seen it."

Since external objects are thus impossible, it is consciousness alone, appearing in fragmentary parts, that is postulated for the sake of all conventional usage regarding the known and the knower. As it has been said:
"Neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor air, nor space, nor anything else;
consciousness alone, the witness to the playful display of the drama of the universe, unfolds everywhere."
Furthermore:

"The cognition of difference—appearing in the form of blue, yellow, pleasure, and pain—is manifest within a single consciousness, just as the thought 'this woman has a deep navel and high breasts' appears upon a flat painted panel. Thus [it is said].
Thus, because it is devoid of a second thing called an external object, non-duality (advaita) remains as nothing other than consciousness-only, which is established by direct experience.
{3.2 Uttarapakṣa}

This doctrine of the non-duality of consciousness (*vijñānādvaita*) contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); for external objects such as blue and so forth, which possess a form distinct from consciousness, are perceived by direct perception as being ultimately real. If it is argued that such direct perception is erroneous, we say no, because there is no sublation (*bādhaka*). If it is argued that the very absence of the characteristics of the cognized and the cognizer (*vedya-vedaka-lakṣaṇābhāva*), which has already been mentioned, constitutes the sublation, then the Yogācāra who speaks thus must establish the momentariness, the self-cognizability (*ananyavedyatva*), and the multiplicity of streams (*nānā-saṃtānatva*) of cognitions through inference alone, since these are not established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). This is because, just as with the Supreme Brahman, self-awareness is absent regarding cognitions insofar as they are momentary, self-cognizable, and of multiple streams—given their [alleged] permanence, omniscience, and unity. Otherwise, the establishment of Brahman itself would be unavoidable through that same [self-awareness]. Therefore, let the establishment of momentariness and so forth be by means of inference alone. And thus, if the characteristic of being cognizable were somehow established in respect to momentariness and the like, then the proof of the momentariness etc. of the cognitions under discussion would be accomplished by inferential knowledge (*laiṅgika-jñāna*), and not otherwise.

Furthermore, there is no definition of the object of cognition (*vedyalakṣaṇa*) that is free from the aforementioned defects, since the Proponent of Cognition (*vijñānavādin*) has stated that [characteristics] such as its arising are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Since the inference of the momentariness of consciousness and so forth is possible through the cognition of that [consciousness], it cannot be claimed that such [inference] is impossible elsewhere in the case of external objects, for there is in every respect no distinction between them.

Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*): Knowledge, which is the subject of dispute, has as its objective support an object distinct from its own nature, either directly or through a causal series; because it possesses the form of the apprehended and the apprehender; like the inference of another mental continuum (*saṃtānāntara*) and so forth. If it is argued that there is a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender appearing in erroneous knowledge (*viplava-jñāna*), we say no; for then the proof of another mental continuum and the like would also be subject to the fallacy of deviation. Indeed, the manifestation of distinctions in activity and speech is not non-erroneous; if it were, the reason [of the opponent] would be non-deviant. If the reason consisting of activity and so forth, which is considered true during the waking state, were non-deviant, then the reason consisting of the aforementioned forms of the apprehended and the apprehender would likewise be non-deviant, since it is intended to be exactly the same.

If it is argued that the distinction between mental impressions (*vāsanā*) is understood through the cognition regarded as true, that is equally applicable elsewhere. For just as in the waking state, because the impression of an external object is most firm, there is the conceit of truth regarding the cognition of its form; whereas in states such as dreaming, because that impression lacks firmness, there is the conceit of untruth regarding that perception—so too, in an undisturbed state, because the impression of the cognition of another continuum (*saṃtānāntara*) is most firm, there is the conceit of truth, while elsewhere, due to its lack of firmness, there is the conventional designation of untruth. Thus, let the distinction between impressions be understood, but not [the existence of] another continuum. If that were not accepted, how could the momentary destruction of one's own continuum and so forth be established? Therefore, even going to the furthest extent, some cognition must be sought that relies upon its own desired reality. Consequently, this proponent of false views, who composes a treatise for the sake of convincing others, actually obstructs the cognition of consciousness and the knowledge of reality for those who possess it; thus, this [argument] amounts to nothing. Therefore, since the proof of the form of the cognized and the cognizer establishes that the cognition of an external object has a support distinct from its own nature, the absence of the characteristics of the cognized and the cognizer is not a sublater, because it has been sublated by a counter-argument.

If it is argued: "Surely there exists a sublater (*bādhaka*) of the perception of external objects, because the inference that blue and its cognition are non-different due to their necessary simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*), like the two moons, serves as that sublater," we say no, because the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*). If the word "simultaneous" (*saha*) means "at the same time," then the necessity of such simultaneity exists in plurality (*nānātva*), which is the opposite of non-difference. If it is argued that even in non-difference, this necessity exists in the case of the two moons; we say no, because even there, there is a difference according to how they appear. If it is argued that, according to reality (*tattva*), there is indeed non-difference; we say no, because according to reality, even simultaneous apprehension does not exist. In this way, the example would also be deficient in both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*). If the mere fact [of being apprehended] were the reason, then since that exists only in the case of difference, the reason would be contradictory. Furthermore, this reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). Since those who perceive a single object, such as a dancing girl, or those who know another's mind, do not necessarily perceive the other's cognition or that object, the reason is unestablished, as the necessity is unestablished. If it is argued that there is no lack of necessity because the form of the dancing girl is manifold; we say no, because that form is one, since all those present in the assembly attain a consensus (*ekavākyatā*) regarding it. If it is argued that their consensus is merely due to some delusion and that in reality the form is diverse; we say no, for this must be understood by drinking from the vessel of oath (*kośapāna*), not through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since there is no such thing whatsoever.

If it is argued that the inference—"all cognitions are without an objective basis (*anālambana*), because they are cognitions, like a dream-cognition"—serves as a sublation (*bādhaka*) of the present subject, we say no. This is because, since the cognitions of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) in the present case lack an objective basis in their own objects, consciousness-only (*vijñānamātra*) is not established, due to the absence of both the reason and the probandum. Alternatively, if they do possess objects, the reason would be inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*) precisely because of those two [cognitions]. As it was said by the venerable Masters: "If the cognitions of the means of proof and the probandum are without objects, there is no establishment of the reason for consciousness-only."
"Furthermore, the fault of deviation regarding meaningfulness does not apply to that which is accessible to yogis and established for the opponent. (Yuktyanuśāsana 18).

Thus, since there is an absence of all subverting factors, the external object is established by non-erroneous perception; therefore, the doctrine of the non-duality of consciousness contradicts what is observed.

Likewise, [the argument] is contrary to what is desired, because the existence of external objects is established through inference. This is the inference: "External objects exist, because there is the employment of means of proof (*sādhana*) and refutation (*dūṣaṇa*). If it is objected: "How, then, can this prove an external object from a subject that is an existing entity (*bhāvadharmin*)? And why could it not be so? For if it were a property of its existence (*sadbhāvadharmatva*), it would follow that it is unestablished (*asiddha*), just like that [external object] itself. If it were a property of its non-existence (*tadabhāvadharmatva*), then by this very fact the non-existence of that [object] would be established, resulting in a contradiction (*viruddha*). And if it were a property of both, there would be the consequence of inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*). [Reply: No; for we admit this [reason] precisely as being devoid of the alternatives of being a property of either one [existence or non-existence] or of both. If it is asked: "In that case, how is it that this serves as a logical mark (*liṅga*) only with respect to the existence of the external object, and not also with respect to its non-existence? [Reply: No; because the rule of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva-niyama*) applies only to that [existence]. Even in the case of a property of the subject (*dharmidharma*) such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), its capacity to produce cognition (*gamakatva*) regarding "impermanence" (*anityatva*) is established for that very reason [of invariable concomitance], and not merely by virtue of being a property of the subject. Otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since [the property of being a subject-property] would apply even to cases such as "originating from the same branch" (*ekaśākhāprabhavatva*).

In this context, the *sādhana* (proof) is the establishment of the fact that blue and so forth are consciousness (*saṃvedana*); the *dūṣaṇa* (refutation) is the negation of their being external objects (*bahir-artha*). The *prayoga* (formal application) of these two is their elucidation. Such as: "Blue and so forth are not distinct from consciousness, because they are cognizable by it, like its own nature"; and: "Blue and so forth are not insentient (*jaḍa*), because they appear [in cognition], like pleasure and so forth. If it is asked: "How can this [blue] be untenable in the absence of an external object? [The answer is: Precisely because it is a particular (*viśeṣa*) of an external object. For in the absence of that [general category], its particular cannot exist, just as one understands that in the absence of a tree, there is no *śiṃśapā* tree. If it is argued: "It is not a particular of that [external object], because its form is superimposed (*āropita*)," [we reply]: No; for from that which is devoid of all causal capacity, neither the desired nor the undesired would be established. If it is argued: "Even if not superimposed, this is merely consciousness (*bodha*) and not an external object," [we reply]: No; because for the person being instructed (*pratipādya*), that [consciousness] does not exist [as an external object]. If it is argued: "[It exists] for the instructor (*pratipādaka*)," [we reply]: How then could the person being instructed understand the subject matter (*prakṛtārtha*) from that [instruction], since one cognition cannot logically produce another? Otherwise, the postulation of distinct cognitions for each individual would result in futility. Therefore, it is logically established that this is indeed a particular of an object; thus, the establishment of the external object is valid. Consequently, it was rightly stated that the doctrine of the non-duality of consciousness (*vijñānādvaita*) contradicts what is accepted [by the proponent himself].
<Thus concludes the Examination of the Doctrine of the Non-duality of Consciousness> {4.
Examination of the Doctrine of the Non-duality of the Variegated}.

By this, the non-duality of the variegated (*citrādvaita*) is also refuted; for even in that system, external objects are denied, whereas external objects have been established through both perception and inference. Enough of this digression. In every respect, the doctrine of the absolute internal object is proven to be untrue, as it contradicts both what is perceived and what is accepted.
Because it lacks any means of valid cognition, every statement of those who maintain the non-duality of consciousness is mere idle chatter; therefore, it should not be heeded by the wise.

The non-duality of cognition cannot be true, because it contradicts both what is perceived and what is accepted; furthermore, it is certain that this [non-dualism] does not constitute a refutation of the *syādvāda*.

{5 Examination of the Cārvāka Doctrine} Now, among the doctrines that propound multiple [conflicting] meanings, the Cārvāka view is first of all contradicted by both what is perceived and what is accepted. For this is their asserted position—
{5.1 The Prima Facie Argument}:
In this world, first of all, no one among the Sugatas and others can be established as omniscient.
If the Sugata is omniscient, what proof is there that Kapila is not?
If both of them were omniscient, how could there be a difference of opinion between them?

Because of this statement [in the *Tattvasaṅgraha*, verse 3129], neither scripture (*āgama*) nor reasoning (*tarka*) exists as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), due to defects such as mutual contradiction; therefore, how could Dharma be established? As it has been said:
"Reasoning is unstable, the scriptures are diverse; he is not a sage whose word is authoritative."
"The reality of Dharma is hidden in a cave; the path is that by which the great multitude has gone" (Mahābhārata).

Then, there is a certain authoritative teacher in the form of a deity, namely Bṛhaspati himself, because he provides instruction on the principles of earth and so forth as established through direct perception. For instance: there are only four principles—earth, water, fire, and air. From these, when transformed into the shape of a body, consciousness arises—just as the power of intoxication arises from the mixture of flour, water, molasses, and *ghātakī*—due to the effort of the tendons, the lute, the staff, the thumb, and the fingers, like the charming sound produced by them. That consciousness, which consists of those [elements], functions under such designations as "the living being" (*jīva*) or "the self" (*ātman*) from the time of conception until death. Prior to conception and after death, it is absent.

Consequently, there is no existence after death; and because there is no one who exists after death, there is likewise no world beyond. In the absence of a world beyond, people—like children, indifferent to the pleasures of this life and subject to deceit and fraud for the sake of experiencing happiness in that other world—undergo manifold and futile suffering by expending their bodies and wealth. Thus it has been said: "As long as one lives, let one live happily; there is no escaping the reach of death.
Once the body has been reduced to ashes, how can there be a return?"
The Agnihotra sacrifice, the three Vedas, the triple staff, and smearing oneself with ashes—
Bṛhaspati says these are merely a livelihood for those devoid of intelligence and manliness.

Those of base intellect, seeking false pleasure, who out of delusion disregard the great seal of woman (*strīmudrā*)—which belongs to the god whose banner is the sea-monster (*makaradhvaja*) and brings about the perfection of *nirvāṇa*—are themselves utterly destroyed by that very [woman], reduced to ashes, plundered, some made to wear five tufts of hair, and others turned into matted-haired ascetics or *kāpālikas*. Furthermore: Alas, the deafening drum-beat of stupidity belonging to those fruitless, fraudulent heretics, who seek the bliss of some other "supreme liberation," is such that they abandon these women—who are languid from the weight of their breasts, whose eyes are moist and rolling with passion, and who in some places resound with songs sung in the fifth note (*pañcama*) of the Malaya breeze! (Source unknown). Thus it is said.

{5.2 The Counter-Argument} This Cārvāka doctrine is first of all contradicted by perception (*pratyakṣa*), because we perceive through direct observation that earth and the other elements stand in a relationship of material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) toward one another; thus, the thesis that they are entirely distinct principles (*tattvāntara*) is established as being in contradiction with perception. Furthermore, even if they were distinct principles while maintaining a mutual relationship of material cause and effect, it would follow that a sprout and so forth must also be distinct principles from a seed and so forth.

Nor is it unestablished that there is a mutual relationship of material cause (*upādāna*) and effect (*upādeya*) among them, because water and fire arise respectively from specific types of earth such as the moonstone (*candrakānta*), the sunstone (*sūryakānta*), and wood; and because the mineral collyrium (*añjana*) and pearls are directly perceived to arise from specific lamps and water, or wind from specific types of earth such as palm-leaf fans, since otherwise one would be guilty of denying what is directly observed.

Likewise, the position that the soul (*jīva*) does not exist is also contradicted by perception; for the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*), which consists of various transformations such as pleasure, pain, joy, and despair, is established as existing even without logical reasons, because it is incontrovertibly experienced through the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*). As it is said: "A reason should indeed be stated for that regarding which the minds of men are deluded;
for the wise do not take up a mirror to see the ring on their own hand. (Source unknown).

Furthermore, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of the soul (*jīva*), whose nature is cognition, is not unestablished; for if cognition were not self-cognizing, it would follow that it does not exist at all, due to the absence of a cognizer. If it were apprehended by another cognition, then the postulation of yet another cognition to apprehend that one would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If that [infinite regress] is not postulated, then it is impossible to speak in such a manner [of its existence]. Nor is its apprehension possible through inference (*anumāna*), because [the opponent] does not accept that [as a means of knowledge], and because it would result in a contradiction regarding the number of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, self-awareness must be accepted. And since, in that case, the soul’s status as an enjoyer—a unique characteristic—is directly realized through self-awareness, this doctrine of Bṛhaspati contradicts what is perceived.

The non-commonality (*asādhāraṇatva*) of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) is not unestablished, because it is impossible for insentient things such as the body and so forth. For the status of being an enjoyer is not possible for the insentient body, since the body is well-known as the locus of experience (*bhogādhiṣṭhāna*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even a corpse possesses the status of an enjoyer. Nor does it belong to the collection of instruments (*karaṇagrāma*), because that serves as the instrument for the experience and enjoyment of objects. Nor does it belong to the objects of sense, such as sound and so forth, because they are perceived as the objects of enjoyment (*bhogya*). Therefore, since the status of being an enjoyer resides in the self (*ātman*), the materialist (*lokāyatika*) who denies it cannot establish the status of being an enjoyer anywhere at all.

If it is argued that the status of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) is possible for consciousness—which inheres in the body as a composite of earth and other elements, which extends from conception to death, and which pervades all particular instances of sentience—because it is distinct from the body and its constituents; then let that very thing be the substance of the self (*ātman-dravya*), since its existence is logically established both prior to birth and after death. The consciousness under dispute is beginningless and endless, because its absolute distinction from the body, senses, and objects—which are composites of earth and the other elements—is otherwise inexplicable. For there is no effect that is absolutely distinct from its cause, given the inherence of qualities such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth. If it is argued that consciousness is not absolutely distinct [from matter] because it also possesses the inherence of qualities such as existence (*sattva*); we say no, for even if the principles (*tattva*) were different, that [quality of existence] would still persist, leading to the undesirable consequence that earth and the other elements would be non-distinct. The various principles of earth and so forth are indeed distinct, because they lack the inherence of a single transforming substrate (*ekavikāri-samanvaya*), just as there is a distinction between the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) and other types of non-existence. Now, is there an inherence of a single transforming substrate between consciousness and the material elements, by virtue of which they would not be distinct as separate principles? Therefore, the absence of the inherence of a single transforming substrate constitutes their distinction, and that alone constitutes their status as separate principles. This establishes that consciousness is beginningless and endless. Thus, this very Self—well-known as beginningless and endless, manifesting in various forms such as joy and sorrow, perceivable by each individual, consisting of both difference and non-difference in every body, and incapable of being denied—awakens the one who seeks to reject it; so enough with this exertion. Consequently, it is proven that the doctrine of the Cārvākas contradicts direct experience.

By this, that which is contrary to what [the opponent] desires is also established, because the self has been proven to be beginningless and endless, and because it will be further established through refutations, figurative designations, and so forth. As it has been said:

"By means of the signs taught by the Jina—accepted by many pure words, consisting of refutations and figurative designations, and characterized by being beyond contradiction—the true nature of existence is brought to light. (Source unknown)

For example—the very statement of negation, "the soul does not exist," indicates the existence of the soul in its primary sense, because affirmation and negation are impossible in the case of that which is non-existent (*nirūpākhyam*). Just as the negation "there is no jar here" reveals the existence of the jar in another location, so too the non-existence of the soul—which is indeed existent by way of its fourfold nature consisting of its own essence and so forth—is logically possible only through its fourfold nature consisting of other-essence and so forth, and not otherwise.

If it is argued that even for things such as the horn of a donkey, which are of the nature of absolute non-existence, there is the possibility of them being objects of negation; we say no, because we observe the negation of a horn—which exists on the head of a cow or similar animal—on the head of a donkey or similar animal. Therefore, it is well-established that the establishment of a negation occurs through the cognition of something that exists.

Likewise, in the case of a painted man and the like, the figurative conception (gauṇakalpana) that "this is a living painting" indicates the existence of a soul by way of primary function (mukhyavṛtti). This is just as in the expression "the boy is a lion," where the state of being a lion in the boy refers to the existence of a lion characterized by a specific genus and so forth. Therefore, it is beyond reproach that the primary [reality] is established through figurative conception.

Similarly, the pure term "soul" (jīva) possesses its own meaning by way of primary function, because it is a pure term, like any other term established by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). Consequently, from its status as a pure term, it is also established that "the soul exists."
Likewise, because it is approved by many distinguished people and because it was composed by authoritative persons, the proposition "the soul exists" is well-established.

Furthermore, there is indeed a difference between the material elements (*bhūta*) and consciousness (*caitanya*), because they appear respectively as external and internal, are characterized by contradictory properties such as childhood and passion, and are apprehended by distinct means of knowledge as being different substances. If they were non-different, their non-perception at different locations would imply that even earth, water, fire, and air—which have transformed into the shape of the body—would be one and the same. Moreover, according to the principle that "the effect must resemble its material cause," since consciousness lacks the qualities of solidity, fluidity, heat, and mobility that characterize the elements, and since it is impossible for formless consciousness to be the product of a formal (material) cause, consciousness is certainly distinct from the body.

Furthermore, desire arises only when there is recognition; recognition occurs only when there is memory; and memory exists only through prior experience. Thus, prior experience is established. Otherwise, it would follow that a newborn infant on the very day of birth would lack desire for the breast and so forth. Moreover, since we observe some who, having died, declare themselves to have been reborn among the families of *rākṣasas*, *yakṣas*, and other beings, and since the recollection of past lives (*bhavasmṛti*) is experienced by some, the next world also exists. As it has been said:

"Because of the lack of desire for food on that day of birth, because of the absence of the sight of demons, because of the recollection of existence (*bhava-smṛti*), and because of not following after living beings, he is established as the eternal knower of nature (*prakṛti-jña*).

(Source unknown). Thus, even though there is no difference in the causes such as birth and so forth, since a variety of experiences such as pleasure and pain is observed, merit, demerit, and the like certainly exist. In this way, when the next world is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the doctrine of Bṛhaspati—which harbors hostility toward the merit and demerit of the next world—does not please the minds of the virtuous in the slightest; rather, it deserves only censure. And this has been stated by the Masters (*Svāmin*):
"Just as in the combination of intoxicating ingredients, the manifestation of another power occurs in the assembly of the elements; this is a non-divine creation.
Alas, the soft-hearted have been deceived by those devoid of shame and fear, who are satisfied with nourishing their own genitals and bellies!
When the cause for birth and so forth is seen to be indistinguishable, what specific distinction exists among these [beings] for each individual?
If it were by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvataḥ*), why would there not be the establishment of others [as well]? Alas, this is a precipice even for those who are not your followers!

"Alas, those outside your vision wander about, proclaiming that for the world which acts according to its own whims, there is no fault in high states of immoral conduct by its very nature; and they believe that liberation is equal to initiation. (Yuktyanuśāsana 35–37).
Therefore, this Bṛhaspati does not take authority for himself.

As for what was said—"there is no omniscient one," and so forth—that too is mere idle chatter; for it is impossible to establish the non-existence of the Sage who is omniscient through perception, inference, or scripture, since these are admitted to have existence as their object. If some perception were to establish the non-existence of that [omniscient one] simply by not occurring with respect to him, then that very same perception would also imply the non-existence of the perceptions of other persons and so forth, as well as the earth and other objects of those perceptions; thus there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because even the perception of Bṛhaspati and others—along with its objects—which you yourself accept, would be proven to be non-existent.

Now, if it is thought that another perception establishes itself as well as its own objects such as earth and so forth—because it operates toward them—and therefore there is no consequence of its non-existence; then an omniscient being (*sarvajña*) would also establish himself through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), as well as objects such as heaven (*svarga*) and the unseen force (*apūrva*). Thus, how could his non-existence be proven? Furthermore, regarding other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whether they consist of his own words in the form of causal discourse (*hetuvāda*) or non-causal discourse (*ahetuvāda*), he alone would be their establisher. So, from where is the proof of his non-existence? If you ask, "What is the proof for the existence of an omniscient being who establishes both self and others? [we reply: For one who maintains that self-perception is the sole means of valid cognition, what is the proof that there exists another perception having both self and others as its object? Such a recognition is established elsewhere as well; thus, perception does not indicate his non-existence, for it is difficult to avoid the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, is the absence of omniscience established by perception in some place, at some time, for someone; or everywhere, at all times, for everyone? In the first case, one is merely proving what is already accepted by the opponent. In the second case, one who perceives through direct experience the absence of omniscience everywhere, at all times, and for everyone, would himself be omniscient. This being so, the Cārvāka’s statement regarding the non-existence of an omniscient being is self-contradictory.

Nor is inference a means of proving that non-existence, because he himself does not accept it; for how could one who, while refuting inference itself, seeks to prove the non-existence of an omniscient being by means of inference alone, not be insane?

Thus, because there is no subverting evidence, an omniscient being exists. And that [omniscient being] is determined—by the exclusion of all other possibilities—to be none other than the Blessed Lord Arhat, the proponent of *syādvāda*, because his words are not contradicted by logic or scripture, whereas the speech of others is contradicted by both reason and tradition. Consequently, the Dharma and liberation taught by him alone are established; for it has already been demonstrated that the Cārvākas lack any valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to refute him, and mere idle chatter is unworthy of consideration by those who possess discernment. Therefore, it is settled that the Cārvāka doctrine is false, as it contradicts both what is perceived and what is accepted as authoritative.
The entire speech of the Cārvākas, who do not perceive direct perception for themselves or others,
would be mere idle chatter and thus should not be heeded by the wise.

The doctrine of the Cārvākas is not true, because it is subverted by what is seen, what is unseen, and what is desired; and it is certain that there can be no refutation of the Syādvāda by means of that [Cārvāka doctrine].

{6. Examination of the Buddhist Teaching} Likewise, the teaching of the Tathāgata is also contradicted by what is seen and what is accepted. For the Tathāgatas, accepting the very nature of the disintegration of all entities at every moment as their essential characteristic, declare thus—{6.1 Pūrvapakṣa}:

The five aggregates, beginning with form (*rūpa*), are themselves the realities. The atoms of form, taste, smell, and touch—which are excluded from those of their own and other classes and are mutually unconnected—are the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). Pleasure, pain, and so forth are the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*). Cognitions that are conceptual (*savikalpaka*) and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) are the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). There are exactly five types of conceptualization (*kalpanā*): genus, action, quality, substance, and name; these correspond respectively to the examples: "a horse," "it goes," "white," "bell-possessor," and "that which is so-called. Thus, that which is accompanied by such conceptualization is conceptual cognition, while that which is devoid of it is non-conceptual. Furthermore, names such as "tree" and so on are the aggregate of designation (*saṃjñāskandha*). The latencies (*vāsanā*) of knowledge, merit, and demerit are the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). These are the five aggregates: form, sensation, consciousness, designation, and formations.

Among these, the successive moments of consciousness arise from each preceding specific state of mind. Functioning in the relationship of material cause (*upādāna*) and effect (*upādeya*), they produce subsequent moments of the same kind. Being mutually unmixed, lacking any underlying substrate, disintegrating moment by moment, and partless, they are nonetheless—due to the power of delusion—assailed by the three forms of cognition: the grasped (*grāhya*), the grasper (*grāhaka*), and self-awareness (*saṃvedana*). To a mind deceived by the production of a continuous succession of similar moments arising rapidly without the intervention of heterogeneous ones, they appear to exist as a continuum and thus give rise to the designation "self. In this regard, even the recognition of identity (*ekatva-pratyabhijñāna*) is insufficient to establish permanence, for it is observed in cases such as nails and hair that have been cut and grown back again, despite the absence of identity between the prior and subsequent states. Thus, these moments exist devoid of any unity persisting through the three times. However, through the excellence of the cultivation of knowledge and detachment, when ignorance and craving (*avidyā-tṛṣṇā*) cease, the subsequent moments of consciousness no longer arise because they lack the necessary causal potency. This cessation of the continuum through a substrate-less destruction (*niranvaya-vināśa*) is liberation (*mokṣa*). As it is said: "The extinction of the self is like the extinguishing of a lamp. Thus it has been stated:
"Beyond a single moment, the body, the senses, and the intellects do not persist;
the aggregates (skandhas), lingering for but a moment, proceed like the flame of a lamp.

Thus, the means to that liberation consists of donning the saffron robes, shaving the head and beard, maintaining celibacy, and so forth. Likewise, those seeking liberation must understand the four categories known as the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

In this regard, there are innate, physical, mental, and adventitious sufferings. Among these, the innate consists of hunger, thirst, fear arising from the mind, and so forth. The physical arises from the imbalance of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*pīnasa*). The mental is produced by such things as reproach, contempt, and the frustration of one's desires. The adventitious is produced by cold, wind, heat, lightning strikes, and the like. These moments of consciousness (*cittakṣaṇa*) characterized by suffering are called the "suffering" of those in cyclic existence (*saṃsārin*). Ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), which serve as the causes for the bondage that generates that suffering, are designated by the term "origination" (*samudaya*). Therein, ignorance is the non-comprehension of the true nature of reality. Craving is the desire for the attainment of desired sensory objects and the avoidance of undesired ones. Cessation (*nirodha*) is liberation, characterized either by the arising of a continuum of consciousness free from outflows (*anāsrava*) through the destruction of ignorance and craving, or by the termination of the [defiled] continuum. Likewise, the path (*mārga*) is that which serves as the cause for liberation.

And that [path] consists of eight factors characterized by rightness (*samyaktva*), conception (*saṃjñā*), the conceived (*saṃjñin*), vocal and bodily action (*vāk-kāya-karmānta*), effort (*vyāyāma*), livelihood (*ājīva*), stability (*sthiti*), and meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Among these: * *Samyaktva* is the vision of things as they truly are. * *Saṃjñā* is the expressive word; the *saṃjñin* is the object expressed. * Vocal and bodily actions are the activities of speech and body. * *Antarvyāyāma* is the retention of vital air (*vāyu-dhāraṇā*). * *Ājīva-sthiti* is the maintenance of life until the end of one's lifespan. * *Samādhi* is the cultivation of the truths: "All is suffering," "All is momentary," "All is selfless and empty.
