Through the excellence of this [cultivation], upon the disappearance of ignorance and craving, moments of mind free from outflows (*anāsrava*) arise, illuminating all phenomena. That is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the yogi. And that yogi, having taught the Dharma to lay practitioners for as long as his life lasts, attains his own nirvāṇa at the end of his life—like the extinguishing of a lamp—due to the non-arising of a subsequent moment of consciousness.
Just as a lamp that has reached extinction goes neither to the earth nor to the atmosphere,
neither to any cardinal direction nor to any intermediate direction, but simply attains peace through the exhaustion of its oil;
so too the living being that has reached extinction goes neither to the earth nor to the atmosphere.
Neither toward any direction nor toward any intermediate point does he go; through the destruction of delusion, he attains absolute peace.

{6.2 Uttarapakṣa}

This doctrine of the Sugatas (Buddhists) is, first of all, contradicted by perception (*dṛṣṭaviruddha*). This is because their own intended *svalakṣaṇa*—defined as consisting merely of atoms that perish without leaving a trace—is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which manifests in the form of gross, stable, and common characteristics. Indeed, atoms characterized by subtle, momentary, and unique forms do not appear in direct perception, since it is only jars and other objects possessing gross, stable, and common forms that manifest therein.

If it is argued that when atoms appear in perception as being extremely close yet unjoined, conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*)—due to some cause of error—conceals them by displaying an unreal form such as "grossness" both within itself and in others, like the illusion of [hair-tufts] and so forth; this is not so. For it would follow that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is erroneous both externally and internally, which entails the consequence that it lacks the quality of being non-erroneous and free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*). This would result in the flaw of the impossibility of the definition: "Direct perception is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous" (Nyāyabindu 1.4).

If it is argued that this is not a fault because the definition of perception applies to the direct perception of atoms (*paramāṇu*), we reply: no, because atoms never appear in a perceptual cognition. Indeed, neither any worldly person nor any investigator directly perceives atoms, just as they do not perceive objects remote in space and time; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of denying one's own experience. Thus, these atoms do not present themselves to perceptual cognition, yet they wish to claim the status of being perceived; they are like those who buy goods without paying their price.

Furthermore, atoms cannot be objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for their direct realization. If it is argued that non-conceptual perception exists, we say no; for that which is non-determinative in nature lacks validity due to its deficiency in non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*). To explain: that which is deficient in non-contradiction is not a valid cognition, such as the vision of poison by one who is ignorant; and the vision postulated by the Buddhists is likewise deficient. For non-contradiction consists precisely in the formation of an intention, thinking "it is thus" or "it is variegated. As it is said [in the *Pramāṇavārttika*, Pramāṇasiddhi 3]: "Non-contradiction [occurs] through the communication of the intended object. And this communication does not belong to that which is non-determinative, because if it did, the same consequence would follow even for the vision of poison by an ignorant person.

If it is argued that even a perception which is itself non-determinate (avyavasāya) is reported because it generates a determination (vyavasāya), we say no; for a determination is impossible, since its own nature cannot be established from any source whatsoever. Even if the nature of a conceptual construction (vikalpa) were established through self-awareness (svasaṃvedana), it would entail the consequence that it requires another conceptual construction, just like the perception of the unique particular (svalakṣaṇa) of blue and so forth.

If self-awareness were to establish its own nature as a definitive cognition independently of any further determination, then even the perception of a thing (*vastudarśana*)—namely, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—would be established in that same way, since there would be no difference [between them]. And if that were so, what would be the need for a subsequent determination? Alternatively, if the perception of a thing required a determination, then the self-awareness of the nature of that determination would likewise require another determination, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Even if one conceptualization were established by another conceptualization, that too would require establishment by yet another; thus, the infinite regress remains exactly as it was. Consequently, a definitive cognition (*vyavasāya*) itself would not be possible, such that perception could attain the status of a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) through its production thereof.

Or, even if some kind of determination (*vyavasāya*) were possible, its production would not be possible from that [perception], because a determination cannot arise from what is non-determinative, just as a horse does not arise from a donkey. Furthermore, if one imagines a determination to arise from a perception that is devoid of verbal expression (*abhilāpa*), why would the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) not produce such a determination, since it too is itself devoid of verbal expression? To claim that perception is the cause of determination, yet color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth are not, is a statement that is poorly established.

If, however, it is held that even from non-conceptual perception (*avikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) there arises a conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of a conceptual nature—just as soot arises from a lamp and the like, since it is observed that an effect can arise even from a cause of a different genus—then let such a perception of a conceptual nature likewise arise from that very object.

If it is argued: "How can perception—which consists of the conceptualization of universals (*jāti*) and so forth—arise from an object that is devoid of the conceptual constructs (*kalpanā*) of universals, substances (*dravya*), qualities (*guṇa*), and actions (*kriyā*)?"—then the same objection applies: "How can conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which consists of the conceptualization of universals and so forth, arise from a perception that is itself devoid of those [constructs]? If it is argued: "There is no fault, because conceptual construction has universals and so forth as its objects," we say: No; for, just like perception, it is contradictory for that [conceptual construction] to have universals and so forth as its objects. Furthermore, it would follow that the real entity (*vastu*) itself arises from that [conceptual construction], and thus its status as the cause of determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*) is indeed untenable.

If it is argued that, through the manifestation of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of a determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*), even a non-determinate perception (*avyavasāya*) serves as a cause for a determinate cognition; this is not so. For, by that logic, the object itself would necessarily be the cause of that [determinate cognition], and thus there would be the undesirable consequence of not postulating perception—which is like a useless internal tumor—as a cause. Furthermore, the non-discrepancy (*avisaṃvāda*) of perception would be merely figurative if it were a cause of determinate cognition, since such non-discrepancy is logically established primarily for the determinate cognition alone through its direct communication of the intended object. Moreover, validity does not belong to perception on that basis, because it would then follow that even the sense-contact (*sannikarṣa*) and other factors would possess validity. Therefore, it is correct that perception is not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*) due to its lack of non-discrepancy. As it has been said:

"Like the sight of poison, for the ignorant person, every perception that is devoid of conceptual construction (*akalpanātmaka*) would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it lacks non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*). (Siddhiviniścaya 1.24). Thus, in the absence of validity, its status as direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*) is far removed; for that [status] is characterized by that [validity], and it is untenable in its absence. Therefore, due to the absence of direct perception, perception is not capable of manifesting atoms.

Nor is it inference; for that [inference], which is preceded by the perception of a logical mark (*liṅga*), is impossible in the absence of perception. Nor is it scripture (*āgama*), because it is not accepted that words have real entities as their objects. Thus, due to the absence of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could there be the apprehension of an object? In the absence of that, the entire range of objects of knowledge (*prameya*) consisting of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as propounded by others would be untenable. Consequently, the great undesirable consequence—that the world is indeed empty—falls upon the Buddhists who hate the doctrine of manifoldness (*syādvāda*). As it was said by the venerable Svāmi Samantabhadra:
"That which is not accessible to perceptual cognition cannot be known through an inferential mark (*liṅga*), nor is it the object of that mark;
nor is there any connection with words regarding its domain. Alas, what is the understanding of those who do not hear [this]? (Yuktyanuśāsana 22).

Consequently, the opponents' thesis that "atoms appear first" is undermined, as is their thesis that "subsequently, gross forms and so forth are perceived through conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). This is because even prior [to such a sequence], gross forms and so forth are seen by perception—just like blue and the like—and because conceptualizations of gross forms and so forth are cognized, just like conceptualizations of blue.

Therefore, let even sensory cognitions not have particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their objects, but rather let them perceive only coarse forms and the like; for conceptualization is impossible regarding what has not been perceived, and because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

For just as no conceptualization of yellow and so forth arises with respect to blue because they have not been perceived, whereas a conceptualization of blue does arise because blue has been perceived, in the same way, let there be no arising of conceptualizations of coarseness and so forth for one who does not perceive them; rather, let there be only the arising of conceptualizations of particular characteristics from the perception of particular characteristics.

But this is not the case, because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises only with respect to coarse forms and the like. If, on the other hand, you maintain that even in the absence of the perception of coarse forms and the like, the arising of their conceptual construction occurs solely by the force of beginningless predispositions (*vāsanā*), then, likewise, even in the absence of the perception of blue and other forms, the conceptual construction of blue and so forth would arise solely through the power of those predispositions. Consequently, there could be no determination of blue and other forms; similarly, how could the determination of pleasure and the like possibly be established? Furthermore, the establishment of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) would be utterly impossible, since it depends on the arising of a certain ascertainment (*niścaya*) regarding it. Due to the non-arising of that [ascertainment], its non-establishment is all the more certain, just as in the case of the "power to attain heaven" or the "distinction from the form of the object. Even the principle that "the cognition of the nature [of consciousness] is intrinsic" (*svarūpasya svato gatiḥ*) would not be proven if such an ascertainment does not arise, just as in the case of the non-duality of Brahman (*brahmādvaita*); thus, everything falls into ruin.

Therefore, based on some form of certainty regarding the determination of the intrinsic nature of blue and so forth, and through the ascertainment of grossness and the like, one must accept that the determination of forms such as grossness exists in the object from the perspective of ultimate reality; otherwise, no determination whatsoever could be established. Consequently, these [forms] cannot be merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), because conventionality—being of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—has already been refuted previously. Thus, the entire statement of the Śākyas, which was previously cited as a formal proposition, is disregarded by the wise.

Is it not the case that gross forms and the like are not ultimately real, because there exist subverting arguments? To explain: a gross form is a composite whole (*avayavin*), and a common form is a universal (*sāmānya*). Now, the existence of a single composite whole in multiple parts, or of a single universal in multiple individuals, is asserted by others. This [existence] must occur either partially or by its entire self in each substratum, since no other mode is possible. If it is argued that "inherence (*samavāya*) is the other mode," we say no; for there is no difference in meaning between the two statements, "it exists in things that are inseparably established" and "it inheres. In that regard, a single entity existing in many cannot exist in each locus partially, because it is partless. Nor can it exist by its entire self, because that would entail a multiplicity of composites and so forth; for there would be as many composites as there are parts, since they would each exist by their entire self. If one were to suppose that composites and the like possess parts, then even there the dilemma of their mode of existence and the resulting infinite regress would follow. Thus, every composite and so forth would not be a single unity, due to the presence of the subverting argument regarding the defect of their mode of existence. But this is incorrect, because the aforementioned defects apply specifically to those who maintain the doctrine of absolute difference (*bhedakāntavāda*). The same applies to the proponents of the theory of manifoldness (*syādvāda*).

"A single [entity] cannot reside in many [locations] because it lacks parts, or else, because it possesses parts, its unity is lost; thus, there is a fault in the theory of subsistence for one who does not accept [the existence of parts]. This is stated in *Āptamīmāṃsā* 62, as it demonstrates those faults against them.

If it is argued that in this way a fault regarding subsistence (*vṛtti*) would follow for those who maintain the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*), then this consequence does not apply, because there is a partial identity (*tādātmya*) [between the whole and its parts] in the case of non-absolutism, just as in the case of cognition possessing the forms of the cognized and the cognizer. For just as cognition has an identity with the forms of the cognized and the cognizer—since they cannot be separated from it—it is impossible to say whether [this identity] is "by one part" or "in its entirety," such that the dilemma would result in cognition having parts, being manifold, or leading to an infinite regress; likewise, the identity of the whole (*avayavin*) and so forth with their parts and so on is also due to the impossibility of separation, and thus it is neither "by one part" nor "in its entirety" individually. Therefore, the Tathāgata (Buddha) might indeed refute subsistence if the parts and the whole were entirely distinct, but he would not do so even when there is a partial identity between them.

As for what else has been stated here—that the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) does not possess a gross form because the connection between atoms is unestablished; for if they were connected by a single part, there would be a division of spatial directions (*digbhāgabheda*), resulting in the six atoms meeting simultaneously at six points and thus falling into having six parts; whereas if they were connected by their entire essence (*sarvātmanā*), the aggregate (*pracaya*) would result in being no more than a single atom—this objection would apply to those who maintain the absolute oneness of atoms, but not to the proponents of the doctrine of manifoldness (*syādvādins*). For the Naiyāyikas and others believe that "atoms do not relinquish their atomic nature even in the state of aggregation, just as they do in their isolated state," whereas the *syādvādins* do not hold such a view, whereby that defect would attach to them. This is because they accept a connection consisting of the transformation into the form of an aggregate (*skandha*)—in some sense (*kathaṃcit*)—of atoms possessing the qualities of smoothness and roughness (*snigdharūkṣa*), with qualities exceeding the minimum by two or more, whether of different or similar kinds, like flour and water, or like heated pieces of lac.
"From the statement: 'The binding of the smooth occurs with the rough; [this applies] whether the degrees are unequal or equal, excluding the minimum. (Source unknown)

Others must also accept this, for otherwise there would be a contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). This is because atoms, being mutually unconnected, could not possibly perform causal functions such as holding or carrying water. For one who maintains that there is no connection, it would be impossible to pull other parts when one part of a rope, a bamboo pole, or a staff is pulled. Yet all of this does occur, since what appears in conceptual construction is established as being perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), for conceptualization is impossible regarding that which is not perceived; otherwise, as has been largely stated, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, it has already been demonstrated that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as direct perception, that grasps merely unconnected atoms. Therefore, since the causal efficiency of carrying water and so forth cannot be explained otherwise, connection is established.

Furthermore, according to this view, since no connection can be established—either partially or in its entirety—between the various specific manifestations (*nirbhāsa*) of a variegated cognition and a single [unitary] entity, the unity that pervades all the parts of the manifestation of blue and so forth would not be established therein. If one were to postulate a plurality of distinct parts for that [cognition], the conventional usage of "a single variegated cognition" would cease to exist; it would instead be like multiple continua (*saṃtāna*) having different colors as their objects, each existing in its own moment. In that case, what other kind of "specific proximity" (*pratyāsatti-viśeṣa*) could there be based on some form of unity? Proximity of place is inconclusive due to its deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by cold winds and the like; proximity of time is inconclusive because of its over-extension (*anaikānta*) to all objects existing at the same time; and proximity of nature (*bhāva*) is inconclusive because of its deviation from the cognitions of many persons arising from a single object. By process of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), only proximity of substance (*dravya-pratyāsatti*) remains possible. And since that is characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) with a single substance, this specific proximity is simply the basis for the conventional usage of "unity" in the case of a variegated cognition; thus, there is indeed a form of unity in some respect.

Thus, just like a variegated cognition (*citra-jñāna*) established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), no room is found for any defect whatsoever—such as the fault of negating the object desired by the proponent of *syādvāda*—in the case of a thing consisting of both subtle and gross aspects, which belongs to a different category [of existence]. Since the refutation of contradictions and other such flaws in this and all other cases actually serves to set aside the very notion of variegated cognition, what need is there for further anxiety? Consequently, the gross form accepted by the proponents of *syādvāda* is established as the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). By this, the common form (*sādhāraṇākāra*) favored by them is also established as ultimate reality, because the universal (*sāmānya*) characterized as "similar transformation" (*sadṛśa-pariṇāma*), as agreed upon by the *syādvādins*, cannot be rejected; otherwise, since there would be no perception of similarity between mother-of-pearl and silver, how could the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of silver upon it occur, based as it does on that [similarity]? For it has been well said: "Or rather, the form of silver appears in mother-of-pearl due to the perception of a similarity in appearance. (Pramāṇavārttika, Svārthānumāna 44cd)

Nor is there anything other than [the self] by virtue of its similarity [to space], because that nature which is eternal and all-pervasive is not perceived anywhere. Thus, the stable form accepted by the proponents of *syādvāda* is indeed the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because—just as a single variegated cognition simultaneously pervades multiple forms—the pervasion of multiple forms by a single entity such as the self is established even through succession. This has been stated by Bhaṭṭa Akalaṅkadeva: "Just as one [entity] might produce or pervade objects located in different places simultaneously, so too might one [entity] produce or pervade objects existing at different times successively. (Laghīyastraya 37)

Furthermore, because there is a contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) if preceding and succeeding moments were entirely without continuity (*niranvaya*). Indeed, causal efficiency is not possible under the doctrine of absolute momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣayaikāntapakṣa*); for if external and internal objects were to perish without leaving any residue, it would follow that an effect is without a cause, which establishes a contradiction regarding its production.

If it is argued: "Since the subsequent moment arises from the preceding moment, how can the effect be without a cause? We reply: No, because causality is untenable for that which does not reach the time of the effect, just like something that has long since passed away.

[Objection: "But surely even that which arrives at the time of the effect does not possess causality, because otherwise it would follow that everything existing in the same moment would be its cause. Therefore, only that whose effect conforms to its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is its cause; that which does not conform to positive and negative concomitance is not a cause. [Response: No; for under the doctrine of the absolute momentariness of all things (*kṣaṇakṣayaikānta*), positive and negative concomitance itself is impossible.

Indeed, when a capable cause exists, it is not the case that an effect which subsequently ceases to exist by itself does not follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that cause, just as in the case of an eternal entity. By the mere fact that "when a capable cause exists in its own time, the effect arises, and not when it does not exist," the following would apply to an eternal entity as well regarding the conformity to positive and negative concomitance in the theory of momentariness: because it is observed that when an eternal, capable [cause] exists at its own time—being beginningless and endless—the effect arises at its own proper occasion.

If it is argued that since [the cause] is always eternal and capable, the effect must occur at its own time [only], and how then could it follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [cause]? Then [we reply]: likewise, if the effect occurs only at a certain time of its absence—within an infinite duration before and after the causal moment, which is characterized by its absence—how could it follow that [absence]? The [objection] is the same. If it is argued that if the eternal [cause] produces multiple effects at every moment, its possession of multiple natures (*aneka-svabhāvatva*) would be established sequentially, so how could there be unity? This is an equal challenge for the [proponent of] the momentary: for even a single entity existing for a moment possesses multiple natures because it has diverse effects, like various objects in different moments. Indeed, a plurality of effects is not tenable without a difference in the power of the cause, just as in the case of cognitions of color and so forth. Just as the cognitions of color and so forth regarding a pomegranate or similar object are based on the difference in the natures of color and so forth, so too, from a single momentary entity such as a lamp-moment, diverse effects like the burning of the wick and the drying of the oil are established as being caused by a difference in powers; otherwise, there would be no plurality even for color and the rest.

But surely, since powers cannot be established as being either different or non-different from the possessor of power, they lack ultimate reality; if that were so, then even for form and the rest, since the alternatives of being different or non-different from the substance—which is established by cognition—would be impossible, they too would lack ultimate reality. However, because the proponents of *syādvāda* accept a unique category (*jātyantara*) of object possessing power—just like variegated cognition—the aforementioned fault does not follow.

Furthermore, the claim that form and other [sensory objects] are ultimately real because they appear in perceptual cognition, whereas their causal capacities are not so because they appear in inferential cognition, is also incorrect. This is because it would entail the consequence that momentary destruction, the capacity to attain heaven, and so forth, would lack ultimate reality. Therefore, just as there is no contradiction in a momentary entity performing multiple effects simultaneously despite being a single unit, so too there is no contradiction in a non-momentary entity performing multiple effects sequentially; thus, the stable form is also ultimately real, free from fault.

Thus, since there is an absence of all subverting evidence (*bādhaka*), the ultimate reality (*paramārthatva*) of those things intended as objects—which are not subject to rejection and possess stable, gross, and common forms—is established. Consequently, it is indeed proven that the reality characterized as *svalakṣaṇa* (the particular) is contradicted by non-erroneous perception (*pratyakṣa*) which grasps those [stable, gross, and common forms]. If it is argued: "This is not a fault, because the reality of *svalakṣaṇa* accepted by the Sugata’s followers is inexpressible (*avācya*)," that is inconsistent. For the reality of *svalakṣaṇa* is made expressible by the very word "inexpressible"; thus, one sees that by one's own words, one's own thesis is abandoned.

If it is argued that even by the word "ineffable" (*avācya*), the intrinsic nature of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not expressed, because only a superimposed form of a universal (*sāmānya*) is denoted by it—this is contradictory. For it is a contradiction for the word "ineffable," which denotes an extrinsic form called a "universal," to express the intrinsic nature of the particular characteristic, just as the word "blue" cannot denote yellow. This was stated by the Master [Dignāga] in the *Yuktyanuśāsana*: "And regarding the term 'ineffable,' since there is the state of being ineffable, it is indeed ineffable; otherwise, the thesis would be contradicted."

"If it were [expressed] by its own nature, then the statement that 'that which expresses another's nature expresses its own nature' would be a contradiction" (Yuktyanuśāsana 29). Therefore, the absolute position that [reality] is inexpressible is not superior; thus, in any case, the contradiction with direct perception is difficult to avoid. Consequently, the thesis is well-established: the teaching of the Śākyas is contradicted by what is observed.

Likewise, the teaching of the Tathāgata contradicts what is desired [by the opponent]. This is because, through inference, one establishes that the self and so forth possess some degree of permanence—which is the direct opposite of the desired absolute momentary destruction. For instance: whatever exists is in some way permanent, because existence is untenable in an absolutely momentary entity due to the contradiction of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) occurring either successively or simultaneously. In this regard, the reason (*hetu*) is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); for existence is absent in the case of absolute permanence, just as it is in the case of absolute momentariness. And its absence [in absolute permanence] follows from the impossibility of succession and simultaneity. That impossibility arises because there is no form characterized by the relinquishing and assuming of prior and subsequent natures, nor because there is no nature consisting of multiple powers at once. Indeed, in an immutable (*kūṭastha*) thing, there is no relinquishing or assuming of prior and subsequent natures; nor is there a persisting form (*anvita-rūpa*) from which succession—whether temporal or spatial—could arise. Nor is there a simultaneous multiplicity of natures from which simultaneity could arise, because that would contradict immutability, since an immutable thing is by definition of a single form throughout. For it is said: "That which pervades the three times by virtue of its single form is immutable" (source unknown), and because absolute momentariness without persistence (*niranvaya-kṣaṇikatva*) is thereby refuted. Thus, it is established that [the self] consists precisely of the non-absolutism (*anekānta*) of succession and simultaneity. Even the conceptualization of succession and simultaneity based on dependence upon auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) is not tenable; for if the thing itself lacks a nature of succession or its opposite in relation to those causes, such dependence is impossible.

Nor is it better to say that their dependence on that [cause] applies to its effects and not to what is eternal or momentary; for that would entail the consequence that those [effects] are not actually its effects.

If it is argued that the determination of something as an effect [of a cause] follows from the production of effects from auxiliary causes conjoined with that [cause], and their non-production otherwise; then, if its coexistence with one auxiliary cause were by the very same nature as its coexistence with all auxiliary causes, then because it would produce all effects while producing a single effect, there would be no production of effects in succession. Furthermore, even in the absence of other auxiliaries, because of its coexistence with those [already present], the simultaneous production of all effects would follow. If, however, it coexists with other auxiliaries through different natures, then its possession of multiple natures—functioning both successively and simultaneously—is established; how then could a thing that is either eternal or momentary, and possesses a single nature, be the pervader of succession and simultaneity? For it is perceived that only an eternal thing which possesses multiple natures—successive and non-successive—is the pervader of those two.

By this, it should be understood that the ascertainment of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the subverting evidence (*bādhaka*)—namely, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) regarding the reason in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)—is somehow demonstrated by the operation of perception upon the eternal. Therefore, since [the reason] truly establishes something as being somehow eternal, the teaching of the son of Śuddhodana is proven to be contrary to what is desired.

Likewise, even the Buddhist scripture (*bauddhāgama*), which teaches the performance of good and evil deeds, merit and demerit, hell and heaven, the causes of bondage and liberation in the next world, and the nature of those things that are beyond the senses—such as bondage, liberation, and the fruits thereof—is not authoritative. Since it shares the same author as scriptures that contradict both what is perceived and what is accepted, it is utterly devoid of authority regarding supersensible matters. Thus, the religious practice of the Buddhists does not attain any firm footing. What need is there for more? Whatever is asserted by the Buddhists is entirely false, because their accepted ultimate reality is emptiness (*śūnyatva*).

For instance, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is held by others to consist in the apprehension of an object as connected with a verbal expression. Yet that [construction] does not exist at all. To begin with, there is no connection between the object and the verbal expression inherent in it, because such an expression is absent therein. If it is argued that [the connection is with] an expression perceived at the time of the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*), brought forth by memory; we say no. For if memory were non-conceptual, its object would be a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), and in that case, the bringing forth [of an expression] would be impossible in any respect. If, on the other hand, memory has the nature of a determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*), then by that [memory] too, its own object must be remembered precisely as being connected with a verbal expression. And since that verbal expression would likewise have to be remembered as being connected with another such expression, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, if memory—despite its awareness of an object unconnected to that [expression]—has the nature of a determinate cognition, why should perception not also possess that same nature? This is because one would have to abandon the absolute position that "objects are determined only in dependence upon their specific designations. For it is stated that even a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is determined without depending upon its specific designation.

Thus, due to the occurrence of faults such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) would not be established anywhere in the absence of the recollection of names. This is because conceptual construction consists precisely in the apprehension of an object connected with a name brought forward by recollection. In the absence of conceptual construction, there would be no perception (*pratyakṣa*) anywhere; for even that which is grasped externally or internally by a perception that has not performed conceptualization would be as if ungrasped, like the experience of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣaya*) and so forth. In the absence of perception, there would be no inference (*anumāna*) anywhere, since the latter is preceded by the former. Consequently, all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be absent. In their absence, all objects of cognition (*prameya*) would be absent, because the determination of an object of cognition is impossible when the means of valid cognition have ceased to exist. Thus, everything intended as reality by the Buddhists would be nothing but emptiness (*śūnya*).

And thus, this shameless Buddhist, being devoid of both what is to be abandoned and the means for its attainment, merely utters cries of protest; he is simply worthy of indifference. Enough with excessive detail, for his doctrine is proven false because it contradicts both what is perceived and what is accepted.
Regarding matters that are perceived or accepted, the scripture spoken by the Sugata lacks authority due to contradiction with perception and acceptance;
regarding matters beyond the senses, it lacks authority because of its identity with those [other scriptures].
Because all conceptual construction has ceased and everything has been relinquished, the entire word of the Buddha would be mere idle chatter; therefore, it should not be heeded by the wise.
Because it contradicts both what is perceived and what is accepted [by scripture], the teaching of the Śākyas is not true;
and it is certain that the doctrine of *syādvāda* cannot be refuted by it.
<Thus ends the Examination of the Buddhist Teaching> {7.
Examination of the Sāṃkhya Teaching} Likewise, the Sāṃkhya teaching also contradicts what is perceived and what is accepted as valid. For this is how the Sāṃkhyas explain it:

{7.1 Pūrvapakṣa} This entire world has *pradhāna* as its cause; and *pradhāna* is by nature the state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Thus say their texts: "Sattva is held to be light and illuminating; rajas is supporting and mobile."
The state of equilibrium of the three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—is primordial nature (prakṛti). (Sāṃkhyakārikā 13)

In this regard, that which is desired, illuminating, and light is called *sattva*. From the emergence of *sattva*, only auspicious transformations arise. That which is mobile, supporting, stimulating, or grasping is called *rajas*. From the emergence of *rajas*, only transformations of attachment arise. That which is heavy, obscuring, and the cause of ignorance is defined as *tamas*. From the emergence of *tamas*, only transformations of aversion and ignorance arise. The state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* is *prakṛti*. From *prakṛti* arises the Great One (*mahat*); from that, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*); from that, the group of sixteen; and from five of that group of sixteen, the five gross elements arise. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 22)

Prakṛti is the producer of the world; "the Pradhāna, the manifold progenitor"—these are the designations for Prakṛti. From that Prakṛti, the Mahat arises. The Mahat is the intellect (buddhi) which persists from the beginning of creation until its dissolution. From that Mahat, the Ahaṃkāra arises. It is the object of such cognitions as "I am the knower," "I am happy," and "I am miserable. From that Ahaṃkāra, the sixteenfold group is produced: the five subtle elements (tanmātras)—smell, taste, form, touch, and sound; the five organs of perception—touch, taste, smell, sight, and hearing; the five organs of action—speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals; and the mind (manas). Among those sixteen groups, the five gross elements arise from the five subtle elements.

The order of creation is as follows: from smell, form, taste, and touch arises earth; from taste, form, and touch arises water; from form and touch arises fire; from touch arises air; and from sound arises ether. These are the twenty-four principles (*tattvas*). The twenty-fifth is the individual soul (*jīva*). The twenty-sixth is the Supreme (*parama*); such is the view of the atheistic Sāṃkhyas. According to the theistic Sāṃkhyas, the twenty-sixth is Maheśvara, and the twenty-seventh is the Supreme. Among those principles:
primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is unevolved (*avikṛti*); the seven beginning with the Great One (*mahat*) are both evolvents and evolved (*prakṛtivikṛtayaḥ*).
"The group of sixteen is a modification; the *puruṣa* is neither nature (*prakṛti*) nor a modification" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 3).

Thus, through the discernment of the distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, when *prakṛti* ceases its activity, liberation (*mokṣa*) is characterized by the *puruṣa* abiding in its own essential nature alone, through the application of unmanifest consciousness, like a person in deep sleep. And the means for that [liberation] is precisely the thorough knowledge of the twenty-five principles (*tattva*).
"One who knows the twenty-five principles, regardless of which stage of life (*āśrama*) he may abide in..."
"Whether one has matted hair, a shaven head, a topknot, or long locks, one is liberated; there is no doubt in this," according to the statement [from source unknown].
{7.2 Uttarapakṣa}

This doctrine of Kapila is contradicted by perception. To explain: first of all, the followers of Kapila maintain that all objects other than the *puruṣa* (spirit) consist of *pradhāna* (primordial matter). Now, that *pradhāna* exists at all times because it is eternal; it exists everywhere because it is accepted as being all-pervasive; and it exists in its entirety everywhere because it is held to be entirely without parts. Thus, it follows that "everything exists everywhere. For if one accepts the premise that "the *pradhāna*, which consists of everything, exists in its entirety everywhere," then one must necessarily accept the conclusion that "everything exists everywhere."

If it is argued that this is a case of proving what is already accepted, since the followers of Kapila (the Sāṃkhyas) universally acknowledge that "all exists everywhere," we reply: this is clearly contradicted by observation, because perception reveals only objects restricted to specific places and times. Indeed, everything is not perceived everywhere through perception; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of perceiving even hundreds of herds of elephants on the tip of a finger.

If it is argued that this is not a fault because, even though everything exists everywhere, only that whose manifestation occurs in a particular place is perceived there, while the other remains concealed—thus establishing a distinction between objects being capable or incapable of being seen—the following must be asked: what is this so-called "manifestation"? If it is said to be the perception of what was previously unperceived due to the operation of a manifesting agent (*vyañjaka*), then is that [manifestation] eternal or non-eternal? If it is non-eternal, then it, being previously non-existent, would have to be produced by causes; otherwise, the consequence of its being eternal would follow. And if that were so, then objects such as a jar, being likewise previously non-existent, would have to be produced by causes—which they are not, because that contradicts the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*). To say that manifestation, being previously non-existent, is produced by causes while a jar and the like are not, is merely a statement based on personal preference, as it lacks any logical justification. If, on the other hand, manifestation is eternal, then there would be the perception of everything everywhere at all times, since manifestation would exist eternally.

If, moreover, another manifestation is desired for that very manifestation which was previously hidden and now exists due to causes, then there would be yet another manifestation for that one, and yet another for that as well; thus, due to this infinite regress, the manifestation of a jar or any other object would never occur.

Now, if it is argued that there is no infinite regress because manifestation—which consists of perception—does not depend on another manifestation of that same nature, just as light does not depend on another light; then one must admit that the cause of that [manifestation] obtains its own existence from a further cause, since there is no other mode [of acquisition] than production or manifestation, and the aforementioned fault applies there as well; thus, manifestation would not be established.

Since that [theory] has been effectively refuted even by its own concealment—because the faults already stated for the positions of permanence and impermanence would still attach to it—and because manifestation has been rejected and a third alternative is impossible; thus, since manifestation and concealment are unestablished, the perception of something in some place on account of them is untenable, and everything would be visible everywhere. But this is not the case; therefore, the contradiction with direct perception remains exactly as it was.

Thus, since it is not perceived despite being capable of perception, the Pradhāna does not exist. In its absence, the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest, which have that as their cause, would also not be established; hence, there would be a total non-existence [of everything]. Nevertheless, out of sheer audacity, the process of the creation of the Great Principle and so forth is described. In that case, he must be asked: "Is this Great Principle and the rest the effect (*kārya*) of the Pradhāna, or its transformation (*pariṇāma*)? Regarding the first position, it cannot be the effect of that which already exists; for if it were entirely existent, the cause would be useless, just as in the case of the Puruṣa. As it is said: "If that which is existent is in every way an effect, it ought not to arise, like the Puruṣa" (Āptamīmāṃsā, verse 39). Nor can it be the effect of that which is non-existent.

Because that which is non-existent cannot be produced, because there is the grasping of a material cause (*upādāna*), because there is no possibility of everything [arising from everything], because the efficient cause produces only that for which it has the capacity, and because the effect exists within the cause; thus, the effect pre-exists (*satkārya*). This is because it would contradict one's own established tenet [in the *Sāṃkhyakārikā* 9], and because production from that which is entirely non-existent is logically impossible. As it is said: "If the effect were entirely non-existent, let it not be produced, like a flower in the sky" (*Āptamīmāṃsā* 42).

In the second alternative, the transformations (*pariṇāma*) such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth, belonging to the transforming primordial matter (*pradhāna*), would either be entirely different from it or non-different. In that case, if they were non-different from it, their successive occurrence could not take place, because the transforming matter itself is non-successive (*akrama*). Therefore, if they were different, there could be no designation [of them as its transformations], because no relationship is established and because they would provide no assistance [to one another].

The Pradhāna cannot be the benefactor of its transformations (*pariṇāma*); for if another benefit produced by it were itself an effect, the faults already stated regarding the positions of existence and non-existence would follow. Furthermore, if the transformations were non-different from one another, there could be no sequential production; if they were different, there could be no designation [of them as belonging to the Pradhāna], because no relationship is established due to the absence of mutual benefit. If one were to postulate yet another benefit, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If the Pradhāna were benefited by the transformations, then there would be as many benefits for it as there are transformations. If those benefits were different from the Pradhāna, then the designation "belonging to it" (*tasya*) would also be impossible, because no relationship is established due to the lack of mutual benefit. If there were yet another benefit for that which possesses those [benefits], the same objection would apply, resulting in an infinite regress. Therefore, if those [benefits] were non-different from the Pradhāna, then either the Pradhāna would be divided into as many parts as there are benefits, or the benefits themselves would attain the singular nature of the Pradhāna; thus, the simultaneous persistence of both the Pradhāna and its benefits is impossible.

If it is argued that transformation is neither different nor non-different [from the primal matter], but rather the *pradhāna* transforms solely into the form of the Great One (*mahat*) and so forth—just as a snake appears in the forms of a staff or a coil—this very point contradicts your own desired doctrine of absolute permanence; for if one accepts a transformation characterized by the abandonment of a prior form and the acquisition and persistence of a subsequent form, the nature of being both permanent and impermanent necessarily follows.

Thus, due to the occurrence of numerous such refutations, the twenty-four principles beginning with *pradhāna* do not remain established. Since they are not established, and in the absence of objects of enjoyment (*bhogya*), the person (*pums*) would lack the status of an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) and would consequently cease to exist, for that [status] is his defining characteristic. Therefore, because the principles of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* fail to be established, every principle asserted by the Sāṃkhyas once again becomes a void. How, then, could this be established by perception? It cannot; for just as the earth, mountains, trees, and other entities are not perceived to be composed of Brahman, they are likewise not perceived through perception to be composed of *pradhāna*. Thus, the Sāṃkhya doctrine is proven to be contradicted by what is observed.

Likewise, this [reason] is also contradictory to what is desired by the opponent (*iṣṭaviruddha*). This is because the eternally immutable (*kūṭastha-nitya*) Puruṣa accepted by the followers of Kapila is somehow contradicted by the inference that establishes his impermanence. And this [inference] is as follows: "The Puruṣa under dispute must be impermanent, because he is non-different from impermanent experience (*bhoga*); for whatever is thus [non-different from something impermanent] is seen to be thus [impermanent], just like the nature of experience itself. Nor is the impermanence of experience unestablished, since it is established by the inference: "Experience is impermanent, because it possesses an origin, like cognition."

If it is asked, "How can enjoyment (*bhoga*) be subject to origination?"—it is because it depends on another, just like that [origination]; for it depends upon the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the intellect (*buddhi*), according to the statement: "The *puruṣa* perceives the object as determined by the intellect" (source unknown). If enjoyment did not depend upon the determination of the intellect, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the *puruṣa* experiencing all enjoyments everywhere and at all times. Furthermore, because it is occasional due to its dependence on the proximity of the object of enjoyment, enjoyment is established as non-eternal (*anitya*). Moreover, if enjoyment were distinct from the *puruṣa*, then—just as with space (*ākāśa*) and the like, or as with one *puruṣa* in relation to another—the status of being an enjoyer would be impossible for it. Therefore, if there is no distinction between enjoyment and the *puruṣa*, the *puruṣa* would somehow be established as non-eternal by virtue of having that [enjoyment's] nature. Thus, this proof correctly establishes the non-eternality of the self (*ātman*). Consequently, it is well said: "The Sāṃkhya doctrine contradicts what is desired."

Likewise, the Sāṃkhya scripture—which expounds the four castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*), their respective various prescribed conducts, merit and demerit, the bondage and liberation of the next world along with their causes and fruits, and the nature of those who are bound and liberated—is not a valid authority. Since it is indistinguishable from scriptures that contradict what is perceived and what is accepted, the possibility of its validity regarding supersensible objects and their causes is untenable; thus, the practice of their dharma does not attain stability. What need is there for much more? Whatever is proclaimed by the countless proponents of Sāṃkhya—whether they maintain the existence of a Lord (*seśvara*) or deny it (*nirīśvara*)—all of that is false. This is because, by means of refuting the manifestation and other attributes of all the principles (*tattva*) they assert, their doctrine has been established as being void (*śūnyatva*). Enough of this digression; for the unreality of the Sāṃkhya teaching is proven by its contradiction of both what is perceived and what is accepted.

Regarding perceptible objects, the scripture accepted by the Sāṃkhya lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge because it contradicts what is perceived and what is desired; regarding imperceptible objects, it lacks such status because of its identity with that [same scripture].
The entire doctrine of the Sāṃkhya regarding manifestation, disappearance, and universal dissolution would be mere idle chatter; therefore, it should not be heeded by the wise.
The Sāṃkhya teaching is not true, because it is contradicted by what is seen, what is unseen, and what is desired;
and it is certain that the doctrine of *syādvāda* cannot be refuted by it.
{8. Examination of the Vaiśeṣika Doctrine} Now, the Vaiśeṣika doctrine as well contradicts both what is perceived and what is accepted [by reason]. For this is their underlying intention:

liberation is the abiding of the self in its own nature through the absolute cessation of the nine specific qualities of the self—namely, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impression; otherwise, there would be no ultimate purification of the self.

The knowledge of the true nature of the categories—substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence—through their similarities and differences, as well as the specific performance of ascetic practices such as receiving initiation into the Śaiva and Pāśupata systems, wearing matted hair, and smearing oneself with ashes three times a day, are the causes of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa).

Among these, the substances (*dravya*) are ninefold—earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind—as designated by their general and specific names; for apart from these, no other designations are mentioned. The qualities (*guṇa*) are seventeen as explicitly stated: color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort; and seven more are included by the word "and" (*ca*): gravity, fluidity, viscidity, mental impression (*saṃskāra*), unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), and sound. Thus, there are twenty-four qualities. Actions (*karman*) are fivefold: throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, and locomotion. By the inclusion of "locomotion," whirling, flowing, vibrating, flaming upward, falling obliquely, bending, stretching, and so forth are merely specific varieties of locomotion and not distinct classes. Generality (*sāmānya*) is twofold: higher and lower, being the cause of inclusive cognition. Therein, the higher is "Being" (*sattā*) because its scope is vast; and since it is the cause of inclusion alone, it is generality only. The lower includes "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) and so on, because its scope is limited; and since it is also the cause of exclusion, it is a generality that also receives the name "particularity" (*viśeṣa*). Ultimate particularities (*antyā viśeṣāḥ*) reside in eternal substances; they are indeed particularities because they are the cause of the cognition of absolute exclusion. Inherence (*samavāya*) is the relation between inseparable substrata and superstrata which is the cause of the cognition "here [is this]"; it is the relation of container and contained. Thus has the enumeration of the subjects (*dharmin*) been made without their attributes (*dharma*). The common properties (*sādharmya*) of all six categories are existence, nameability, knowability, and—except for eternal substances—dependence. The five beginning with substance possess inherence and plurality. The five beginning with quality possess the absence of further qualities and the absence of action.
Thus, this manifold variety of similarities and differences constitutes the knowledge of reality, which is the cause of liberation.

For example: upon the successive removal of suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge, there is liberation because each preceding one ceases in the absence of its immediate successor. In this regard, through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), false knowledge is eliminated. When false knowledge is eliminated, the passion and aversion produced by it cease. When those defects cease, the activity consisting of the operations of body, speech, and mind produced by them ceases. When that activity ceases, the birth characterized by the bondage of merit and demerit produced by it ceases; thus, the cessation of the bondage of future karma occurs solely through the knowledge of reality.

However, the complete exhaustion of all previously accumulated karma occurs only through experience and not otherwise. As it has been said: "Karma is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of aeons unless it has been experienced; whatever karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious, has been performed must necessarily be experienced.

Regarding that, there is also this [verse]: "One who knows the nature of the Self, while performing [actions], effects the exhaustion of karma through experience; having acted thus for thousands of millions of ages, one is liberated by that"—this is one position.

"Having obtained many bodies through the power of yoga, the lord of men may traverse the entire earth with them; with some he may enjoy sense-objects, and with others he may perform severe austerity; and he may withdraw them again, just as the sun withdraws its masses of radiance. This is another position: that within a single birth, one experiences the enjoyment of all the fruits previously accumulated by means of multiple bodies.

And from that, through experience, there occurs the exhaustion of all previously accumulated karma and the cessation of suffering divided into twenty-one varieties. If one asks what those sufferings are: "Contact, pleasure and pain, as well as objects, senses, and cognitions—each being sixfold—thus the enumeration of suffering is twenty-one.

Due to the total exhaustion of all merit and demerit, there follows the exhaustion of the intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) which were preceded by them; this is the isolation (*kaivalya*) and liberation of the Self.

This teaching of the Ulūkyas (Vaiśeṣikas) is, first of all, contradicted by perception; for their asserted absolute difference between part and whole, quality and qualified, action and agent, and genus and individual, is contradicted by perception which apprehends their non-difference.

For the whole (*avayavin*) and so forth do not appear in direct perception as being entirely different from their parts and so forth; rather, they appear as being in some sense non-different. Just as a cloth—whose specific state consists of the warp and woof—is non-different from its threads, or as the appearance of blue and other colors occurs in a variegated cognition, or as the various forms such as a rag are non-different from the person walking, or as childhood and other stages are non-different from the person, or as the action constituting a specific state is non-different from the object possessing the universal, or as the universal characterized by similarity—which is a property of that object—is non-different from it, so too [the whole is non-different from its parts]. This is because it is established by direct perception, witnessed by all the world, that these things have attained a state of integration therein.

If it is argued that, due to inherence (*samavāya*), the composite whole (*avayavin*) and so forth appear as if they were not distinct from those [parts], we say no; for this would entail the consequence that the perception of the composite whole and so forth is erroneous in all cases. This is because, like the vision of a running horse and so forth by one afflicted with cataracts, rapid spinning, travel on a boat, or physical agitation, it would involve the apprehension of an object qualified by a non-existent form. And thus, the definition of perception as "non-erroneous" (*avyabhicāritva*) would become impossible.

Furthermore, these parts and so forth, these wholes and so forth, and this inherence of theirs, are not perceived even once as distinct entities within a perceptual cognition; yet they wish to claim perceptibility for themselves. Thus, they are like those who buy without paying the price, because they claim perceptibility while failing to offer themselves to the perceptual cognition.

Nor does inherence (samavāya) remain established as having the nature described by others, since it is held to be the appearance of non-difference among things that are distinct. To explain: that inherence, which is intended by others to be eternal, all-pervading, and of a single form, must either reside in the inherent relata (samavāyin) or be non-resident.
If it resides [in them], then is it so ultimately or figuratively?
In that regard, inherence does not ultimately reside in the inherent relata, because there is no connection between the two.

For first of all, inherence cannot be the relation between those two, because inherence is unitary; if inherence were to subsist by means of another inherence, that too would have to subsist by yet another, resulting in the fallacy of infinite regress.
Nor can it be conjunction, because conjunction, being a quality, must reside in a substance, whereas inherence is not a substance.

Nor can there be a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), because this [relationship] is observed to function only among objects already connected by another relationship, as in the case of a staff and a man. Otherwise, everything would be both the qualifier and the qualified of everything. Furthermore, there is no connection between inherence (*samavāya*) and its substrata (*samavāyin*) by means of another relationship, since neither conjunction (*saṃyoga*) nor inherence is admitted [as a further connector]. If it were connected by yet another qualifier-qualified relationship, then that too would only function among things already connected by another [relationship], leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Nor can it be unperceived, for that would contradict the doctrine that there are six types of relations. If inherence were connected with the unperceived, then qualities, their substrates, and so forth, would likewise be connected by that very means; thus, enough with the postulation of inherence and the like.
The connection of inherence cannot be established through any further relation.

Now, it might be argued: "We do not maintain that inherence (*samavāya*) has a relation with another relation, which would lead to faults such as infinite regress. Rather, its relation is logical as being intrinsic (*svata eva*), just like the heat of fire, because it is by its very nature a relation, whereas conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the others lack that [intrinsic relational nature]. For the nature of one thing does not belong to another; otherwise, since heat is observed in fire by its own nature, it would follow that water and other things must also possess it. If this is your objection:

That too is mere idle chatter; for it is appropriate to offer an answer by means of intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) regarding the nature of an object established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). As it is said: "If one is questioned regarding an object perceived through direct perception, an answer must be given by means of its intrinsic natures; for when something is seen, what is there that is untenable? Otherwise, by such an answer, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that everyone could establish whatever they desired.

Furthermore, the fact that inherence (*samavāya*) is inherently a relation, whereas conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like are relations by virtue of it, is not established by perception; for its own nature has been demonstrated to be beyond the scope of perception. For this very reason, it is supersensible (*atīndriya*), because—like existence (*sattā*) and other categories—it lacks occurrence within perceptible objects, and because there is no self-cognition directed toward its own self. This is stated in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*. Moreover, there is a contradiction with inference: "Inherence, when being related to another category, is not related by itself, because it is something being related, just like color and so forth."

If, like heat, illumination, and impurity in fire, lamps, dogs, meat, and so forth, inherence (*samavāya*) is the cause of the relation between self and other, then why, by relying on that very same example, would cognition not be the cause of the illumination of both self and other? And in that case, the [inference] "cognition is cognizable by another cognition because it is an object of knowledge" (*prameyatvāt*) would be overturned.

Furthermore, just as for an entity (*bhāva*) whose nature is existence (*sattā*), there is no other connection with existence, so too for inherence (*samavāya*), which is of the nature of occurrence (*vṛtti*) in substances and the like, there is no other occurrence. Therefore, considering that it "occurs in itself" (*svātmavṛtti*), why would one not consider that for cognition (*jñāna*), which is of the nature of awareness (*saṃvedana*) regarding objects, there is no awareness by means of another, and thus it is self-aware (*svataḥ-saṃvedana*)—just like an entity, since there is no difference in their identity (*tādātmya*)? Even if that [identity] is the same, one might argue that by the example of existence, inherence alone has occurrence in itself, but cognition does not have self-awareness; this is merely displaying a view fabricated according to one's own whim. For just as in the case of a self-relation, there is no contradiction in an action being directed toward itself in the case of self-awareness as well; otherwise, that consequence would apply there too, because that single [cognition] possesses the nature of both the connector and the thing to be connected.

As for the argument that says: "Inherence does not require another relation because it is inherently a relation. Those things which require another relation are not inherently related, such as jars and the like. This [inherence], however, is not something that is not inherently a relation; therefore, it does not require another relation"—this too is a mere wishful thinking, because it is rendered inconclusive by the case of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). For conjunction is inherently a relation and yet requires another relation. Indeed, if conjunction were not inherently of the nature of a relation, it would be illogical for it to become so through something else, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, this argument has its object sublated by inference: "Inherence requires another relation when it is joined with a distinct category, because it is a distinct category. Whatever is thus is thus, like conjunction. And this [inherence] is so. Therefore, it is exactly like that. Thus, the subject matter of the original argument is refuted by this inference.

Furthermore, just as inherence (*samavāya*) is established as consisting of both difference and non-difference—because it is non-different from its own nature, yet different from the forms of the constituents and the constituted which are not distinct from it—so too, because every entity is non-different from the whole (*avayavin*) and so forth, yet different from the parts that are not separate from it, every object is established as a unique category (*jātyantara*) consisting of both difference and non-difference. This is because objections such as contradiction are removed by the example of inherence; thus, the doctrine of the Arhat is established, since he accepts this, as stated in your own words: "The reality of objects consists of both non-difference and difference. Once his doctrine is established, an entity that is exclusively of the nature of difference—as maintained by others—would be as non-existent as a sky-flower, according to the statement: "A sky-flower is [defined as] either one or the other independently."

Thus, in this way, the inherence of inherence in its inherent substrates could not occur either through itself or through another. Because it lacks such occurrence, inherence does not, in the ultimate sense, reside in its inherent substrates; for others [the Naiyāyikas] admit its independence.

Nor can inherence be established through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), because the grounds for such a designation are absent. If it is argued that the ground for metaphorical designation is the cognition of inherence when the inherent substrates (*samavāyin*) are present—since the cognition of inherence is impossible in a location devoid of inherent substrates—that is incorrect. For if that were so, it would follow that space (*dik*) and the other [eternal substances] are likewise dependent (*āśrita*). This is because, when corporeal substances (*mūrtadravya*) are present and perceptible, there exists the cognition "this is to the east of that" and so forth, which is the mark (*liṅga*) of space; and there exists the cognition of priority and posteriority (*paratvāparatva*), which is the mark of time (*kāla*). Consequently, it would follow that space and time are metaphorically designated as being dependent upon corporeal substances. And thus, the statement "except for eternal substances" would be contradicted, since it would be established that even eternal substances like space and time are dependent by way of metaphorical designation. Therefore, inherence cannot be established as dependent even through metaphorical designation.

Now, if it is held that inherence (*samavāya*) is non-dependent, then inherence cannot be a relation; for a relation is established as such only when it is distinct from its two relata and dependent upon both, just like conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Thus, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Inherence is not a relation, because it is in every way non-dependent. Whatever is in every way non-dependent is not a relation, just like space (*dik*) and so forth. And inherence is in every way non-dependent; therefore, it is not a relation. Nor is the reason here unestablished (*asiddha*), since the dependence of inherence—both in an ultimate sense and by way of metaphorical designation—has already been refuted.

It might be argued: if the substratum (*dharmin*), namely inherence (*samavāya*), is not apprehended, the reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*). If it is apprehended, the thesis (*pakṣa*) is sublated by the very means of valid cognition that apprehends the substratum, and the reason becomes "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). For inherence is apprehended by whatever means of valid cognition [it is known], and by that very same means its status as a relation between things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*) is also apprehended; for it is only the relation of things that are inseparably established that is established by the designation "inherence."

That too is not more convincing; for inherence (*samavāya*), which is characterized by non-separateness (*aviṣvagbhāva*), is understood precisely as something dependent upon that which is apprehended by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps inherence. Moreover, if one were to accept its independence, it would follow that it lacks any relation, thereby establishing the relationship of pervasion (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) between the probans and the probandum. This is because, once the pervaded is accepted by the opponent, the acceptance of the pervader—which is inseparable from it—is demonstrated. Indeed, independence is not unestablished in the case of [directions] such as the quarters (*digādi*) with respect to being unrelated (*asambandhatva*). Nor is the reason inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because no instance of anything independent is known to possess relatedness, and thus there is no occurrence [of the reason] in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). For this very reason, it is not contradictory (*viruddha*). Nor is it countered by an equal argument (*satpratipakṣa*), because there is no inference capable of establishing relatedness even for that which is independent.

For others, there exists no relation of inherence (*samavāya*) by virtue of which the cognition of distinct entities such as a composite whole (*avayavin*) and so forth could occur as non-distinct. Consequently, they would have to be cognized only as distinct. But this is not the case. Therefore, it is difficult for others to avoid the contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, since inherence is impossible according to the manner already demonstrated, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is also impossible, because that [conjunction] cannot be established in the absence of the inherence of the effect in its cause. Thus, in the absence of any relation, not a single entity can be established in the doctrine of absolute difference (*bhedakāntavāda*).

For instance: first of all, in the absence of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) among atoms (*paramāṇu*), there is no production of composite wholes (*avayavin*) through the process beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*); consequently, the four elements (*bhūtacatuṣṭaya*) in their form as effects do not exist. In the absence of those [elements], the four kinds of atoms which are their causes are also not possible, because a cause has its existence inferred from its effect; for it is said that "the error regarding the atom is due to the error regarding the effect, since the cause has the effect as its mark" (*kāryaliṅga*). Likewise, when the four elements are non-existent, time (*kāla*) and space (*dik*) cannot be established, because the cognitions of "prior," "posterior," and so forth, as well as the cognition "this is to the east of that," would cease to exist. Similarly, due to the absence of the conjunction of the drum and the stick with space, sound produced by conjunction (*saṃyogaja-śabda*) does not arise. Since there is no conjunction of parts anywhere, there can be no disjunction (*vibhāga*) either, and thus sound produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja-śabda*) also does not arise. In the absence of these two, sound produced by sound (*śabdaja-śabda*) is impossible; therefore, since all sound fails to arise, space—which is established by that means—is lost. Likewise, because the conjunction of the self (*ātman*) and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is unestablished, qualities such as cognition (*buddhi*) do not arise. In the absence of those, the reality of the self is lost, as the means of establishing the self would be non-existent. Similarly, if cognition does not arise, the mind (*manas*) is unestablished, because the successive arising of cognitions is the mark of the mind; for it is said that "the non-arising of simultaneous cognitions is the mark of the mind. Thus, in the absence of conjunction, all substances (*dravya*) are non-existent.

Alternatively, since inherence (*samavāya*) is impossible in the absence of existence (*sattā*), [existence] would be deprived of all substances. Upon the loss of all substances, the qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), universals (*sāmānya*), and particulars (*viśeṣa*) that depend upon them could not be established, because when there is no substratum (*āśraya*), there can be no superstratum (*āśrayin*), just as there is no cloth in the absence of threads. Thus, for the Vaiśeṣikas, the loss of all objects follows inevitably from the loss of conjunction (*saṃsarga*).

This has been stated by the venerable Svāmisamantabhadra: "The reality of objects, consisting of both identity and difference, must for you be either identical or different; otherwise it would be like a sky-flower. Since the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) lacks any mode of occurrence, it would lack connection, and consequently, all objects would be lost.

When analyzed in this way, parts, wholes, and so forth—which are in every respect non-different—do not exist in themselves, because they would not appear in perception. However, those things which are their opposites—possessing some degree of difference—do appear through perception. Thus, it is established that the Vaiśeṣika doctrine contradicts what is observed.

Furthermore, that [position] is also contradicted by what is desired [by the opponent]. To explain: the followers of Yoga establish that the world is created by Maheśvara, arguing that "the body, organs, the world, and so forth, which are subjects of dispute, have an intelligent cause because they are effects, like a jar. However, this is contradicted by inference, because there exists an inference that subverts it. That inference is as follows: "God is not the creator of the body and so forth, because he is bodiless; whoever is thus [bodiless] is thus [not a creator], just like the self; and this [God] is likewise; therefore, he is exactly so. Nor is the reason (*hetu*) here unestablished (*asiddha*), because it is impossible for him to possess a body. For a body composed of parts cannot be eternal. Even if his body were eternal, if it were not preceded by an intelligent cause, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reasons such as "being an effect" and so forth. If, on the other hand, that [body] were preceded by an intelligent cause, then by postulating successive bodies, one would fall into the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Moreover, if each preceding body were the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) for the production of each subsequent body, then since such a thing is well-known among all transmigrating beings, the postulation of God would be useless. Furthermore, even in the production of the worlds and so forth to be enjoyed by himself, those [transmigrating beings] themselves can be established as the efficient causes. Thus, the reasons—namely, being an effect, having insentient material, and possessing a specific configuration—would fail to be conclusive. And there is contradiction with scripture (*āgama*), as in: "Neither pleasure nor pain touches one who dwells bodiless" (Chāndogyopaniṣad 8.12.1).

Thus, his bodilessness being established, God cannot be the creator of bodies and so forth, because it is impossible for him who lacks a body and organs to perform such creation. Even if he were such [a being], it would not be contradictory for actions to have him as their efficient cause, despite their insentience, since in every respect this would involve a departure from the observed analogy. For just as the potter and others, who possess bodies and organs, are seen in the analogy to be the instigators of jars and the like, yet [in your view] the creation of bodies, organs, and worlds is postulated to be instigated by a bodiless, organless God—so too, even though actions are insentient, let the analogy of an intelligent being be set aside by that same postulation, as there is no distinction between the two cases.
