It might be thought: "Even for one possessing a body, it is observed that only a potter and the like who possess intellect (*buddhi*), desire (*icchā*), and effort (*prayatna*) act as the instigators of causal factors (*kāraka-prayoktṛtva*); for this is not seen in one who lacks such intellect when attempting to produce an effect such as a jar, nor is it perceived in an intelligent being when desire has ceased, nor is it found in one who possesses desire when effort is absent. Therefore, since it is possible for the Lord (*Īśvara*)—who is without body or organs, yet possesses intellect, desires to create, and possesses effort—to be the instigator of all causal factors at all times, there is no deviation from the analogy. For corporeality and its opposite are not essential factors (*aṅga*) regarding the instigation of causal factors; indeed, there is no complete equality between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the argument (*dārṣṭāntika*), because of the contradiction regarding their specific differences. This is incorrect, because intellect and the other qualities are impossible for him as well. The Lord does not possess the triad of knowledge, the will to act, and effort, because he is bodiless, like a liberated soul (*muktātman*); thus his lack of these qualities is established. If it is argued that although there is no difference in being bodiless, only those liberated souls who have a beginning (*sādi-mukta*) are devoid of intellect and so forth, while the beginningless liberated Lord (*anādi-mukta-īśvara*) is not, we say no, because an "eternally liberated" Lord is not established. There exists a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against that: "The bodilessness of the Lord has a beginning, because it is bodilessness, like the bodilessness of a liberated soul. If it is further argued here that although there is no difference in bodilessness, only the bodilessness of the liberated soul has a beginning and not that of the Lord, we say no, because it is untenable. Since attributes of the Lord such as being the creator of the world and omniscience are themselves subjects of dispute, it is impossible to assert a distinction [of the Lord] based on those very attributes. Even if one were to accept it despite this, why would one not accept that among effects like jars, cloths, bracelets, crowns, and so forth—which are indistinguishable in being products—only some (jars, etc. have an intelligent cause while others (the earth, mountains, trees, etc. do not? Furthermore, even for one who has made no prior convention, a distinction is possible between the earth and so forth, which do not produce the notion of having been "made," and jars and so forth, which do. Thus, since the possession of intellect, desire, and effort is unestablished in the case of bodilessness, and since the capacity to instigate all causal factors is impossible if those are unestablished, it is well said that the Lord is not the creator of the body and other such things.

Nevertheless, if by sheer audacity it is asserted that God is the creator, then does God inflict hundreds of diverse and terrible sufferings upon living beings or not? If he does not inflict them, then there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reasons such as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) and so forth. If, on the other hand, the view is that he does inflict them, that is impossible. For here, some sage or other virtuous person who is not omniscient, yet whose passion and hatred have perished, does not inflict pain upon others; indeed, such a one is worthy of worship even by the great seers. How then can those possessed of discernment conceive that the Blessed Maheśvara—the omniscient Lord who is free from passion, hatred, and delusion—is the one who, being worshipped by the great seers, inflicts a succession of causeless, unbearable, and manifold fierce sufferings upon living beings and thus torments the three worlds? Or, if he were to do so, his nature would be nothing but that of an exceedingly fierce and unprecedented demon, rather than the state of Maheśvara praised by the great; therefore, his performing such an act is inconceivable.

If it is argued that God does not produce suffering for living beings, we say no; for if even the evil karmas that are the causes of suffering were created by God, then He alone would be established as the cause of suffering, and the faults already adduced against that position would follow as a consequence. If those [karmas] were not created by Him, then let it be that the body, the sense organs, and so forth are also not His creation, since there is no distinction between them. Furthermore, the reasons proving the existence of God are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of [the role of] karmas; for even if karmas have non-intelligent causes, their production, persistence, and activity are possible through their being effects, their performing purposeful functions, and their inherent tendencies. If one must necessarily admit karma even after postulating a God, then let karma alone be accepted as the cause of the body, the sense organs, and so forth; what is the use of this God who is contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such that the opponents' laborious effort at a long succession [of causes] might be avoided?

If it is asked, "How can insentient *karmas* produce bodies, organs, and so forth, which are suitable for various experiences?"—then let it be explained how intoxicants such as *unmatta* and *madirā*, or *kodrava* grain and the like, produce diverse effects such as intoxication; or how specific types of magnets perform actions such as attracting and rotating iron. If you say, "Because it is observed to be so," then by that very same principle, the aforementioned assault upon the nature of things (*svabhāva*) should also be set aside. Furthermore, this is because [the existence of *adṛṣṭa*] is inferred from the reasoning: "There exists an unseen cause (*adṛṣṭa*) for pleasure, pain, gain, loss, and so forth, since their connection with visible causes is otherwise inexplicable. Nor should one suspect that, in this way, the denial of God (*Īśvara*) would also follow because He too is inferred, for that inference is vitiated by numerous fallacies.

To explain: regarding the proof of the body, organs, the world, and so forth, by means of their being effects and the like—does this seek to establish that they have a single intelligent cause, or multiple intelligent causes? In the first case, the argument is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because [the world] has multiple causes, such as architects and patrons in the case of a palace and similar structures. In the second case, it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because bodies and other things to be enjoyed by various living beings have those beings as their causes, since they are produced by the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of those very beings.

By this, it is stated that in the proof of a general intelligent cause (*buddhimatkāraṇasāmānya*), there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*); for even by the logic of a "presumption based on the subject" (*adhikaraṇasiddhāntanyāya*), the specific [cause] intended by him is not established. If it is argued that there is no fault because the object of proof is a general property qualified by a specific one, we say no; for one cannot escape the two alternatives of a general property being based on either a perceived or an unperceived specific instance. If the general property based on a perceived specific instance is what is to be proved, the desired conclusion is frustrated. If the general property based on an unperceived specific instance is what is to be proved, it follows that the example would be devoid of the property to be proved (*sādhyaśūnyatva*). Even if one proves a general property based on a specific instance other than the perceived one for the sake of illustration, how could the specific instance intended by oneself be established?

If it is argued that this follows from the principle of *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (the established conclusion of the topic), one must ask: what is this so-called *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*? It is defined as: "When, upon the establishment of one thing, another matter within the same context is also established, that is an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.30). Therefore, if it is claimed that once the general fact of the world having an intelligent cause—based on specific observed and unobserved particulars—is established, then by virtue of the context, it follows that the creator of the world is necessarily established as one who possesses the capacity for its creation, who is the director of all causal factors (*kāraka*), whose power is never impaired, who is omnipresent, and who is specifically characterized by being bodiless and so forth; [we reply: this might be so, provided that the general category of an intelligent cause—which is invariably concomitant with the aforementioned specific observed and unobserved particulars—could be established through some means as being capable of creating the entire world and as the director of all causal factors, even with the specific qualities of omniscience and the like. But it is not so established. This is because it has been proven and supported that such a cause is pervaded only by multiple intelligent causes, specifically those who serve as the instrumental causes for bodies and other things to be used by themselves. Furthermore, if the probandum (*sādhya*) is "having an omniscient and dispassionate creator," the reason (*sādhana*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the case of a jar and the like. Moreover, the illustrative example (*nidarśana*) lacks the probandum. If the probandum is "having a passionate and non-omniscient creator," it results in a contradiction of one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*). Furthermore, the reason "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) in the case of bodies and the like, since they are causes in some respect. However, "being an effect in some respect" is contradictory (*viruddha*), because it proves the opposite of the probandum—that there is an intelligent cause in some respect—rather than the intended probandum of an intelligent cause in every respect. Likewise, the subject (*pakṣa*) would also be sublated by inference, since there exists a subverting inference previously stated: "God is not the creator of bodies and the like, because He is devoid of knowledge and other faculties, just like a liberated soul. Thus, the fact that the world has an intelligent cause is not established, because there is no proof and there is the possibility of sublation. Therefore, it is well said that the Vaiśeṣika doctrine contradicts what is desired.
<Thus concludes the Examination of the Vaiśeṣika Doctrine> {9.
Examination of the Naiyāyika Doctrine} {9.1 The Prima Facie Argument (Pūrvapakṣa)}

The Naiyāyikas, whose established tenets are similar to those of the Vaiśeṣikas, declare as follows: "The attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results from the knowledge of the truth regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the objects of cognition (*prameya*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), example (*dṛṣṭānta*), tenet (*siddhānta*), members of inference (*avayava*), deliberation (*tarka*), ascertainment (*nirṇaya*), discussion (*vāda*), sophistry (*jalpa*), cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), quibble (*chala*), futile rejoinder (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.1) Furthermore, through the three yogas—bhaktiyoga, kriyāyoga, and jñānayoga—one attains liberation respectively as *sālokya*, *sārūpya*, *sāmīpya*, and *sāyujya*.

In that regard, Bhaktiyoga consists of performing service to Maheśvara for as long as one lives, with a mind focused on him, thinking, "He is my master; I am his servant. From that, liberation in the same world (sālokya) arises.

The practice of austerity (*tapas*) and self-study (*svādhyāya*) constitutes *kriyā-yoga*. In this context, austerity is the endurance of internal and other forms of suffering for the purpose of removing madness and similar afflictions; self-study is the repetition of the mantra that expresses the Lord (*īśvara*). Both of these are to be practiced for the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma, and for the attainment of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). From that *kriyā-yoga*, liberation occurs as either similarity of form (*sārūpya*) or proximity (*sāmīpya*) [to the Lord]. The application of the mind to the Lord by one who has understood the categories of existence is *jñāna-yoga*.

The continuous contemplation and thorough reflection upon the principle of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvaratattva*) is *īśvarapraṇidhāna* (devotion to the Lord). The eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga*) of that yoga are: restraint (*yama*), observance (*niyama*), posture (*āsana*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and absorption (*samādhi*). Among these, the *yamas*—non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), celibacy (*brahmacarya*), non-stealing (*asteya*), and so forth—are the causes for the pure functioning of the person, which are not limited by place, time, or circumstance. The *niyamas*—such as worship of the gods, circumambulation, twilight prayers, and recitation (*japa*)—are specific meritorious practices that depend upon place, time, and circumstance. *Āsana* is the binding of the body for the purpose of overcoming the afflictions (*kleśa*) that obstruct yogic practice; it includes postures such as the lotus (*padmaka*) and the cross-legged (*svastika*). *Prāṇāyāma* is the cessation of the movement of the abdominal air, practiced gradually through the methods of exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*). *Pratyāhāra* is the complete withdrawal of the mind from all objects that are adverse to *samādhi*. *Dhāraṇā* is the fixing of the mind upon a particular location. *Dhyāna* is the one-pointedness of the mind directed toward that object. *Samādhi* is the state in which consciousness remains fixed on a single point due to the excellence of meditation, like a lamp in a windless place. These limbs of yoga should be practiced with diligent application by one seeking liberation, having taken refuge in supreme devotion to the Great Lord (*maheśvara*). Then, in a short time, one perceives the Blessed One whose nature is incomparable. Having seen Him, one attains the unsurpassed beatitude of union (*sāyujya-niḥśreyasa*).

{9.2 The Counter-Argument} This position of the logicians contradicts both what is perceived and what is accepted. Since the contradictions with perception and inference are established here as well by the very same method just explained immediately above, no separate effort is undertaken here to establish those contradictions.

Furthermore, among the categories accepted by them, since the sense organs, the intellect, and the mind function as instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by means of accomplishing the apprehension of objects, it is untenable for them to be included within the objects of knowledge (*prameya*); otherwise, their nature would be established as being both one and many. Moreover, since doubt and the like cannot be consistently classified as objects of knowledge, and because error and non-determination are perceived as entities distinct from the sixteen categories beginning with the instruments of knowledge, the system of sixteen categories is not tenable.

In the same way, since the doctrines of the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas have been established as being contradicted by both perception and scripture (*dṛṣṭeṣṭaviruddha*), even the *Yaugāgama* (the scriptural tradition of the Yogas) is not authoritative. This is because it teaches—just like the system of the four castes and stages of life—the various practices enjoined therein, merit and demerit, the next world, bondage and liberation, the causes and fruits thereof, and the nature of those bound and liberated; yet, as it is indistinguishable from an *āgama* contradicted by perception and scripture, its claim to authority regarding supersensible matters and their causes is untenable. Thus, their performance of religious duty does not attain stability. What need is there for many words? Whatever is asserted by the followers of Ulūka (*aulūkya*) and the logicians (*tārkika*), whether worldly or Vedic, is all false. Since the impossibility of the conjunction of all the categories (*tattva*) they accept has been established, resulting in the conclusion that everything is void (*śūnyatva*), enough of this prolixity. For it has been proven that the systems of the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas are untrue due to their contradiction with perception and scripture.

Regarding perceptible objects, because it contradicts what is seen and desired, the scripture accepted by the Yogas cannot be a valid means of knowledge; regarding imperceptible objects, [it cannot be valid] because of its identity with that [same scripture].

Because it would entail the abandonment of all associations and the loss of all objects of experience, every statement of the Yogas would be mere idle chatter; therefore, it is not to be heeded by the wise.
The Yoga doctrine is not true, because it contradicts both what is perceived and what is accepted [by scripture];
furthermore, it is certain that the Syādvāda cannot be refuted by it.
<Thus ends the Examination of the Naiyāyika Doctrine> {10.
Examination of the Mīmāṃsaka Doctrines of the Bhāṭṭa and Prābhākara Schools} Now, the doctrine of the Mīmāṃsakas as well is contradicted by both what is perceived and what is accepted.

{10.1 Pūrvapakṣa} First, among the Mīmāṃsakas, the Bhāṭṭas say this: there are exactly eleven categories—earth, water, fire, air, space, time, ether, self, mind, sound, and darkness; since qualities, actions, universals, and so forth, which depend upon them, are possible as being identical with them because they have that very nature, they are not separate categories. Thus, from the knowledge of the true nature of these categories, the destruction of karma occurs. But the Prābhākaras, however—
In the system of the Guru (Prabhākara), there are nine categories: substance, quality, action, universal, number, similarity, power, inherence, and sequence.

In this system, the substances (*dravya*) are earth and so forth; the qualities (*guṇa*) are color and so forth; the actions (*kriyā*) are throwing upward and so forth; the genus (*jāti*) is existence (*sattā*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), and so forth; number (*saṃkhyā*) is oneness, duality, and so forth; similarity (*sādṛśya*) is one thing residing in a *gavaya* with respect to a cow as its counter-correlate, while the similarity residing in a cow with respect to a *gavaya* as its counter-correlate is another; power (*śakti*) is capacity, and it is indeed only inferable; inherence (*samavāya*) is the relation between quality, substance, and so forth; and sequence (*krama*) is the production of one thing immediately after the production of another, beginning from the first oblation up to the final oblation. Thus, there are exactly nine categories (*padārtha*). They declare that the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results from the knowledge of the true nature of these [categories].

Furthermore, having studied the Veda, understood its meaning, and determined the sequence for the performance of the obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), optional (*kāmya*), and prohibited (*niṣiddha*) rites prescribed therein, one who engages in the performance of those prescribed duties attains the accomplishment of heaven (*svarga*) and liberation (*apavarga*). The obligatory performance consists of the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), recitation (*japa*), and the libations (*tarpaṇa*) to the gods, sages, and ancestors, performed at the three junctions of the day. The occasional performance consists of rites carried out on occasions such as the new moon (*darśa*), the full moon (*paurṇamāsa*), and eclipses. Both of these must be performed according to rule. Why? Because of the scriptural statement: "By failing to perform the enjoined action, one is tainted by sin" (source unknown). The optional performance pertaining to this world includes rites such as the *putrakāmyeṣṭi* sacrifice for one desiring a son. The optional performance pertaining to the next world includes rites such as the *jyotiṣṭoma*. Prohibited performance includes such acts as "one practicing sorcery should sacrifice with the *śyena* [rite]. Having determined the sequence for these, he who engages in the performance of those prescribed rites among them attains both heaven and liberation.
Moreover:

"One who has acquired wealth by righteous means, who is devoted to the knowledge of reality, who is fond of guests, who possesses faith, and who speaks the truth—even such a householder is liberated. (Source unknown)
Because of this statement, there is no fixed rule that those seeking liberation must necessarily take up the life of a wandering mendicant (*pravrajyā*).
Even in that regard: "One should not engage in optional (*kāmya*) or prohibited (*niṣiddha*) acts for the sake of liberation."

"One should perform the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites with the desire to avoid transgression (*pratyavāya*)," so say the Bhāṭṭas. To this, the Prābhākaras replied: "Since one is impelled to perform the obligatory and occasional rites by the desire to avoid transgression, and since these two are also subsumed under the category of performance for a desired end (*kāmya*), their performance is not even considered by one who desires liberation. This constitutes the second part, the *uttarapakṣa*.

This position of the Mīmāṃsakas is, first of all, contradicted by perception. The Bhaṭṭas and Prābhākaras, known as Mīmāṃsakas, maintain that objects such as the earth are manifested through universals such as "existence" (*sattā*). They assert that this universal, existence and so forth, is in every respect eternal, partless, unitary, and all-pervading. However, this is contradicted by direct perception, because a universal characterized by a similar transformation is perceived through the senses as being impermanent, non-omnipresent, and multiform—possessing many aspects just like color and other qualities—due to its nature as consisting of multiple individuals. Indeed, a single universal is not perceived through the senses in distinct locations among individuals, in the manner that a bamboo pole is perceived in a pillar or similar object; for even when an individual is produced or destroyed, the universal would have to be neither produced nor destroyed, which is why it could never be perceived. Thus, this universal, whose nature is propounded by others, fails to establish itself within perceptual cognition while yet wishing to claim perceptibility; therefore, due to this refusal to pay the price [of consistency], it becomes merely an object of ridicule for the wise.

Nevertheless, if the ritualists (*yājñika*) should, out of impudence, maintain that it is exactly so, then we reply to them: for a universal that exists in one individual (*vyakti*) in its entirety, there could be no existence in another. For its existence there [in the second] would have to occur either by moving to that place, by being produced together with the individual, by its presence in that place, or by possessing parts. First, its existence in another individual cannot be due to movement, because you admit that it is devoid of action (*niṣkriyatva*). Furthermore, would it go there by abandoning its previous individual or without abandoning it? Not by abandoning it, because if it abandoned the previous individual, it would follow that the former individual, having lost its "cowness" (*gotva*), would become a non-cow. Nor by not abandoning it, because it is impossible for this partless entity to move—just like color and other qualities—without abandoning the individual with which it is associated. Indeed, the transfer of color and other qualities to another substratum is never observed while they remain unseparated from their original substratum. Nor can it be due to being produced together with the individual, because that would entail the consequence of the universal’s impermanence. Nor can it be due to its presence in that place, because prior to the production of the individual, this [universal] could not exist there without a substratum; or, if it did exist separately, it would contradict the principle that it exists only in its own substratum. Nor can it be by way of possessing parts, because you assert its partlessness (*niraṃśatva*). Consequently, it follows that the universal would be non-existent in any other individual.

The opponent’s argument: Whatever has not arisen in a certain place, nor existed there previously, nor arrived from another location afterwards, does not exist there—just as a horn does not exist on the head of a crow. And such is the case with a universal (*sāmānya*) in relation to an object such as a jar, which arises in a location devoid of it. As it has been said:

"It neither moves [to its new location], nor was it there before, nor does it possess parts; yet it exists afterwards and leaves its former substratum. Oh, what a succession of calamities! (Pramāṇavārttika, Svārthānumāna 152cd–153ab).

Now, one might argue: "This fault belongs only to the proponents of difference (*bhedavādin*), but not to the Mīmāṃsakas, because they accept the identity (*tādātmya*) of the universal and the individual.

If you cite the statement, "If it is asked why this [universal] has identity [with the individual], let it be understood that it is due to its own nature" (*Ślokavārttika*, Ākṛtivāda 47), we reply: for them, this would entail that the universal, like the individual, possesses both unique and common forms; furthermore, it would follow that the universal would be subject to arising and destruction just like the individual.

Nor does it possess the nature of a universal or a common form; furthermore, its association with arising and perishing is not admitted. If that were so, then due to the superimposition of contradictory properties, this [universal] would be distinct from the individuals. And it has been said: "If identity with the universal is maintained, then when an individual is born, the universal would be unborn; likewise, when it perishes, the universal would be imperishable. Why then is its lack of continuity not also accepted?"

If it has not been produced at the birth of the individual, yet has arrived from another substratum, then it did not previously exist in that location; how then could it have become conjoined with it?
If it is not destroyed when the individual is destroyed, nor has it gone to another individual, and it does not abide in a place devoid of them, then tell me: where is that genus?

"If, even when there is a connection with a universal (*jāti*) and so forth, that [connection] is not admitted for the individual (*vyakti*), how could identity (*tādātmya*) be accepted by those whose minds are unclouded? (Hetubinduṭīkā §32).
Thus, because it is vitiated by many such defects, the universal authorized by the ritualists (*yājñika*) would be non-existent, just like a donkey's horn.

As for the proof of its existence stated by others: "The cognition of 'cow' with respect to various individual bodies is based on a single *gotva* (cowness), because it has a single form appearing as 'cow,' just like the cognition of a single cow-individual. (Ślokavārttika, Vanavāda 44)
"Nor does the cognition of a cow arise from a brindled cow, nor does it have something other than that as its objective support,
because it exists even in the absence of that [particular individual], just like the cognition of 'earthen' with respect to a jar" (Ślokavārttika, Vanavāda 45),

and so forth— all of this proves what is already established; for it is established that the recurring cognition has as its objective support a universal characterized by a similar transformation (*sadṛśapariṇāma*).

For we do not deny the universal (sāmānya) as the Buddhists do; we merely do not accept a universal characterized by qualifiers such as eternal in every respect, as imagined by others. This is because, upon investigation, a single entity that is eternal in every respect, indestructible, and omnipresent is found to be impossible.

If it is argued that "existence" (*sat*) and so forth are eternal universals (*sāmānya*) because they are recognized through re-cognition (*pratyabhijñā*), like sound—this is not so; for the reason is contradictory (*viruddha*). This is because it proves something that is in some way eternal, which is contrary to what is intended [by the opponent]. For recognition is impossible for that which is eternal in every respect. This is because the cognition "this is that very same thing" is logically possible only when there is a single entity pervading successive temporal states (*paryāya*); for that which is devoid of succession (i.e., eternally unchanging) cannot be the object of cognitions of "before" and "after."

If it is argued that only the two properties (*dharma*) exist as prior and posterior, and not the common substrate (*dharmin*), then how can there be the cognition of non-difference in the form "this is that very same thing"? For the past and present intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*)—the former referred to by the memory that grasps the past as "that" and the latter apprehended by the perception that delineates the present as "this"—are mutually distinct.

If it is argued that the cognition of both difference and non-difference between those two [the universal and the particular] occurs in some way due to the single universal "Being" (*sat*) and so forth, then its impermanence in some respect is established, because it is not distinct from its own impermanent properties. Indeed, it is not logical for that which is non-distinct from the impermanent to be permanent, just like the very nature of the impermanent; furthermore, because for an entity that is entirely permanent, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is contradicted by both succession and simultaneity. Therefore, that universal "Being" is impermanent because it is subject to specification (*viśeṣādeśa*), like sound. For that very reason, it is manifold, just like that [sound]. If it is argued that the universal "Being" and so forth is one because there is no distinction in the self-referential cognition "it exists" (*sat*) and so forth, we say no; for a total lack of distinction in such self-referential cognitions is unproven, since the cognition "it exists" and so forth does differ according to each individual manifestation (*vyakti*). If it is argued that the specific cognition has those manifestations as its object, then if those manifestations are understood to be entirely different from the universal, the Mīmāṃsaka would have entered the system of the Yogācāras. But that is incorrect, because in their view the relation [between a universal and its instances] has been refuted, and thus the designation "its" (belonging to the universal) would be untenable.

Now, if they are somehow non-different, then it is established that the universal (*sāmānya*) is the object of the cognition of the particular (*viśeṣa*), because it is logical for the universal—which is somehow non-different from the particulars that are the objects of the cognition of the particular—to be the object of that cognition, just like the very nature of the particular itself. Therefore, the universal such as "existence" (*sattā*) is not one alone, nor is it partless, since it is perceived as having parts in some way; for it is logical that what is not a separate entity from the particularized parts should possess parts, just like their own nature. Likewise, that universal is not all-pervading, because it is not perceived in the intervals between individual manifestations. If it is argued that its non-perception there is due to its being unmanifested, then let there likewise be no perception of it there, just as there is none of the individual's own nature. If it is argued that its non-perception is due to its non-existence—because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to prove its existence there—we reply: let the non-perception of the universal also be due to its non-existence, because of the absence of particulars [in those intervals], since there too there is no means of valid cognition to prove its existence, it is not so experienced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and it is like the horn of a donkey and so forth. For the universal is not perceived as one in distinct locations, in the manner that bamboo and the like are perceived in [separate] posts; for if it were to exist simultaneously in multiple distinct locations as its substrates, its oneness would be established, and thus one could prove its existence in the intervals between its substrates. Thus, because of the presence of these many subverting arguments (*bādhaka*), that which is desired by the Bhāṭṭas and Prābhākaras...
May there be well-being.
